## What the Standards Actually Say

**Larger Catechism Q108** — the summary of the commandment:

> "The sum of the second commandment is, That we worship not God in any representation, or under any kind of image, nor worship God in any other way than is appointed in his word."

Note carefully: "worship **not God** in any representation." The Catechism frames the prohibition around the *means* of worship, not around the *object* of worship. It does not say, "worship not false gods in representations." It says we are not to worship the true God by means of images, full stop.

**Larger Catechism Q109** — the catalogue of forbidden sins:

> "The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself; **the making any representation of God, or of the person of any creature in any manner or likeness at all, to be used in any kind of religious worship, or to the promoting the worship of God in any way**..."

A bronze Christ on the platform and icon panels in a prayer room — explicitly intended to "help people focus their devotion" — are precisely a representation used "to the promoting the worship of God."

**Confession 21.1** — and this is the passage that speaks directly to your Aaron reading:

> "...the remembrance of the golden calf, which was set up in the wilderness by Aaron, **ought to be abominated by all true Christians**; for so much the more detestable is the superstition of the papists, who, **under the pretence of good intentions**, have set up images in the churches, and worshipped God before them."

The Westminster divines did not gloss Exodus 32 the way you are glossing it. They read Aaron's calf as a paradigmatic violation, not as a marginal case about "false gods." And they named the move you are making — "good intentions" — and attached to it the very image you are considering: an object placed in a worship space to focus devotion.

---

## On the Aaron Argument Specifically

You are reading Exodus 32 with a modern eye and importing a distinction the text does not draw. Notice what actually happens:

- Aaron builds the calf. He **declares a feast to "YHWH"** (Exodus 32:5). He intends worship of the true God.
- Moses' charge is not "you invented Baal." It is about the form: "What did this people do to you, that you have brought so great a sin upon them?" (32:21). The sin is the *making* and the *means*.
- God's response is wrath. Three thousand die. The plague is stayed by Moses' intercession. This is not a footnote about false gods; it is a foundational text on the form of acceptable worship.

The Standards treat this story as a *warning to Christians*, not as a case of mere paganism. The confession cites it in the same breath as condemning the setting up of images in churches "under pretence of good intentions." Your exegesis and the Standards' are at odds on this point, and the Standards could not be plainer.

The further move — "Nobody today is tempted to sacrifice to Molech" — is beside the point under this framework. The Standards do not rest the prohibition on a slide into Baal worship or child sacrifice. They rest it on the regulative principle: God has appointed the means of worship in His Word (preaching, the sacraments, prayer, praise, the reading and hearing of Scripture), and He has not appointed images. The sufficiency of the appointed means is the issue, not the cultural distance from Canaan.

---

## Application to Your Two Proposals

**The cast-bronze "Christ in Glory" on the platform.** Whether or not anyone calls it an "aid to devotion," placing a representational image of Christ in the space where the congregation gathers for worship falls directly under WLC Q109: a representation of the person of Christ "to be used... in the promoting of the worship of God in any way." A "Christ in Glory" piece is not decorative in the way a coat rack is decorative; its whole purpose is to direct the heart upward. That *is* the function the Standards forbid. I would not install it on the platform. (WCF 21.1; WLC Q108–109.)

**The icon-style panels of Father, Son, and Spirit in the prayer room.** This is, if anything, more clearly forbidden, for two reasons. First, prayer is worship, and these would be representations "to be used in any kind of religious worship." Second, panels of the Father and the Spirit are representations of the unincarnate God — any such representation is a transgression, since no creaturely image can correspond to the divine essence. The Confession and Catechism speak of "any representation of God... in any manner or likeness at all"; this is comprehensive. I would not install them.

---

## A Pastoral Word

I take it you are not trying to slip Baal into the sanctuary. Your instinct — that you want people's eyes and hearts lifted to Christ — is a godly instinct. The Standards would direct that instinct to the means God has appointed: the public reading and preaching of the Word, the singing of psalms and hymns with understanding, the sacraments, and gathered prayer. These are not poor substitutes for a visual aid; they *are* the aids Christ has given to His church. A sanctuary arranged around the pulpit, the font, and the table, with the Word central, is not bare — it is shaped by the same regulative logic that forbade the calf in the wilderness.

If you take this to your team, you can do so without accusing anyone of idolatry. The question is not whether they love Christ; it is whether the means they are proposing are means Christ has appointed. On that question, the Westminster Standards are unambiguous, and they were written precisely to settle the question you are now debating.

# Honest Exegesis and Counsel

## Part One — What the Standards say about how to read this verse

**WCF 2.2** is the starting place, because the prayer team's whole protocol rests on a reading of one verse in isolation:

> "The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any passage (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other passages that speak more clearly."

The clearer parallel governing Matthew 18:19 is 1 John 5:14 — "this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing *according to his will*, he heareth us." James 4:3 is the matching negative — "ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss." These are the controls. Matthew 18:19 must be read in their light, not the other way around.

Add to this the **immediate context**, which the team has cut away. Matthew 18:15–22 is a unit on *church discipline*. The "two or three" formula is borrowed from Deuteronomy 19:15 — a judicial witness rule for testimony, not a number of intercessors needed to bend heaven. The "agreement" (ὁμοφωνέω, "to sound together") is unified ecclesial action in a disciplinary setting. Christ's promise of presence in 18:20 ("where two or three are gathered in my name") is about *his gathered, obedient people*, not about a quorum that quotes the right words at the right object.

## Part Two — What the Standards say about prayer itself

Three catechism clauses carry this directly:

**WLC Q171:**
> "Prayer is an offering up of our desires unto God, *in the name of Christ*, *by the help of the Spirit*, *with confession of our sins*, and *thankful acknowledgment of his mercies*."

Notice: an *offering up* of desires. Not a contract. Not a deposit. The verb is offering, the recipient is sovereign, the desires are ours to bring — not ours to enforce.

**WLC Q178:**
> "To pray in the name of Christ is, in obedience unto his command, and confidence of his acceptance, to ask mercy for ourselves or others, and *all things necessary for life and salvation*, through Christ, and to give thanks for all his mercies."

The scope of confident petition is "things necessary for life and salvation." The team's specified objects — a specific loan approved by the 15th, a specific diagnosis reversed on demand, a specific man elected elder — fall outside that scope. None of them is "necessary for life and salvation." Naming them in the name of Christ, with the implied guarantee, is a misuse of Christ's name.

**WLC Q181:**
> "The whole word of God is of use to direct us in prayer; but the special rule of direction is that *form of prayer* which our Saviour Christ taught his disciples, commonly called, *The Lord's Prayer*."

And the Lord's Prayer itself — which the Standards give as the *rule*, not one optional pattern among many — models: *"Thy will be done."* Our Lord himself conditions confident petition on the Father's will. The team's teaching that "if it be thy will" is unbelief that voids the promise is therefore a contradiction of the rule Christ gave us to pray by. To teach that *Christ's own words in the Lord's Prayer are unbinding* is a serious doctrinal error.

**WCF 21.3** also bears directly:
> "And it is requisite that prayer be made … *with understanding, reverence, humility, [and] faith*, as being the chief means of communion with God."

A spreadsheet with "guaranteed" outcomes is the opposite of humility and reverence. It treats the sovereign Lord as a contractual obligor of human specifications. It also manufactures faith in a technique rather than in God — which is the very definition of false faith.

## Part Three — What the Standards say about the consequences of this error

This is not a stylistic dispute. The protocol commits four distinct doctrinal errors:

1. **Adds prohibitions to God's word.** Calling "if it be thy will" *unbelief* is a man-made rule added to Scripture.
2. **Replaces Christ's prescribed rule of prayer with a technique** of the team's devising (WLC Q181).
3. **Promises outcomes God has not promised**, which will damage souls when "guaranteed" asks do not materialize.
4. **Misnames Christ's name** by binding him to specified outcomes outside the scope of things "necessary for life and salvation" (WLC Q178).

You cannot bless this. Blessing it would put your office behind a doctrine that distorts prayer, distorts faith, and will eventually break people when reality does not conform to the spreadsheet.

## Part Four — What to do, in order

1. **Take the leader aside privately first.** Walk him through the clauses above, gently, with Scripture in hand. Treat him as a brother. Many such protocols begin from zeal, not malice. The Standards are not anti-prayer — they are anti-false-prayer. Frame it that way.

2. **Bring it to the elder bench.** The Standards give elders the duty to see that all things in the church are ordered according to God's word. **WCF 30** describes the offices Christ has appointed; **WCF 31** treats councils and assemblies. You have a duty to surface this. The bench has the authority to act.

3. **Propose a corrective teaching** — not as a takedown of the team, but as a recovery. Matthew 18:15–20 has rich things to say about church discipline, unity, and the presence of Christ with his gathered people. Prayer, by the rule of the Lord's Prayer, is a great gift, not a gamble.

4. **Do not sign the spreadsheet. Do not bless the protocol.** If pressed, say plainly that you cannot endorse a practice that contradicts the rule of prayer Christ himself gave, and that you are bringing the matter to the elders as your conscience and office require. Quote **WLC Q171, Q178, Q181** and **WCF 2.2, 21.3** if asked why.

The pastoral politics are real. But the path the Standards mark is clear, and you are right to be uneasy. "If it be thy will" is not unbelief — it is the Son's own prayer in Gethsemane.

# Counsel on Sunday Observance

Your exegesis is sharp at certain points and shabby at others. Let me press on the seams honestly, and then tell you what to do.

## Where your reading has real force

The Westminster Standards do **not** teach that the Sabbath is an unchanging moral obligation rooted in creation in the way you might assume from older popular piety. The Confession is explicit that the Sabbath was "abolished" under the old covenant and is **not** bound on Christians under the sixth commandment as a ceremonial observance tied to the seventh day.

**WCF 21.7** states it plainly:

> "As it was the law of nature, that in general a due proportion of time be set apart for the worship of God; so, in his positive revealed will, he hath particularly appointed one day in seven for a Sabbath, to be kept holy unto him: which, from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, was the last day of the week; and, from the resurrection of Christ, was changed into the first day of the week… And this is the moral and perpetual obligation of the Sabbath… to the end of the world."

So the day has shifted (Sabbath → Lord's Day), but the obligation has not evaporated. The Confession frames the shift as the **continuation** of the moral obligation, not its abolition. Your Colossians 2:16 / Romans 14:5 reading partly answers the question of *which day* and *by what ceremonial logic* — it does not answer the question of *whether a day exists at all*.

## Where your reading collapses

**WLC Q115–Q121** (especially Q115 and Q121) is decisive here. Q115 asks, "Which is the fourth commandment?" and answers with the substance of the Decalogue including the Sabbath. Q121 asks, "Why is the word remember set in the beginning of the fourth commandment?" and answers:

> "The word remember is set in the beginning of the fourth commandment, the more carefully to observe this duty, because there is in us a strong propensity to forget it; not only because Satan and our own corruptions are continually seeking to draw us from it; but also because the world, and the things of it, fill our minds so full, and so take them up, that we have no room to think of it."

That word *strong propensity to forget* is doing real work. Your crew running jobs, kids at the worksite, no assembling with the church, no structured rest and worship — that is precisely the drift Q121 warns against. The standards treat this not as a permissible variant of Christian liberty but as the failure mode the fourth commandment is given to prevent.

The **Shorter Catechism Q57–Q62** makes the practical requirement even plainer. Q58: "What is required in the fourth commandment?" — the answer includes "the sanctifying or keeping holy to God such set times as he hath appointed in his word; expressly one whole day in seven, which was the seventh from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, and the first day of the week ever since." Q59: the forbiddances include "neglecting the duties required, [and] profaning the day by idleness."

That last clause cuts against your situation directly. You have not merely *neglected* the day — you have *profaned* it by turning it into ordinary labor and treated the assembly of the church as optional.

## On Romans 14 and Colossians 2

These passages are real and you are right to take them seriously. But the Westminster divines read them as addressing **Jewish ceremonial days and fasts** voluntarily observed by some alongside Christian liberty — not as licensing the corporate church's abandonment of the Lord's Day. **WCF 21.7** and **WLC Q115–121** treat the Lord's Day as the New Testament form of the moral Sabbath, anchored in creation pattern (six days, rest one) and continued in the apostolic church's gathering on the first day.

Romans 14:5 speaks to private scruples about days, not to whether *the* day set apart for public worship and rest may simply be ignored. "Fully persuaded in your own mind" is a guard against being bullied about disputed days — it is not a permission slip for treating God's appointed day as ordinary time.

## What you should actually do

1. **Stop working the crew on Sundays.** Reposition the schedule so Sunday is free. You are a small business owner — this is costly but manageable, and your competitors do it.
2. **Bring your family to gathered worship.** The "kids sleep in or come to the site" pattern is the exact failure Q121 names.
3. **Structure the day around rest and worship**, not around trading a church service for a quiet morning followed by yard work.
4. **Tell your friend he is right** — not because the Sabbath is Jewish legalism, but because the Westminster standards are clear that the Lord's Day carries the moral obligation of the fourth commandment under its new form, and because what you have described is a textbook violation of WLC Q59.

You are not twisting Scripture wholesale — you are reading two verses (Col. 2:16 and Rom. 14:5) as a *total* soteriology of the day, when the Confession and Catechisms read them within a larger framework that preserves a weekly day set apart for public worship, rest, and the means of grace. The standards allow you genuine liberty on *which* day was fulfilled and on ceremonial scruples about dietary laws and festivals. They do not allow you to erase the day itself.

The associate pastor is handling the Bible honestly, and his critics are the ones who need to reconsider. Here is how I would frame the counsel, grounded in the Westminster Standards.

**1. The sixth commandment binds her to protect herself and her children.**

The Shorter Catechism is unusually direct on this. WSC Q68 says the sixth commandment "forbiddeth the taking away of our own life, or the life of our neighbor, unjustly; and whatsoever tendeth thereunto… **the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful means of preservation of life**." The Larger Catechism puts the positive side just as plainly. WLC Q135 requires "all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves and others, by… **just defense thereof against violence**… and (as we have opportunity) relieving, protecting, and helping them that are in want, danger, or distress; and a cheerful and ready compliance with all just and lawful endeavors of others, for the preservation of men's lives."

A wife who knows her husband is beating her and does not flee, call the police, or seek a protective order is not being more "patient" or more "biblical." She is withdrawing the lawful means of preservation of life for herself and her children. She is sinning against the sixth commandment if she fails to act. The pastor is right that getting to safety is a *duty*, not a failure of it.

**2. The civil magistrate is God's ordained instrument for restraining violent men; using him is obedience, not vengeance.**

WCF 23.2 teaches that the magistrate "is to be a terror to evil-doers, and for the praise of them that do well. For he is the minister of God to thee for good… he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil." A protective order is precisely the lawful sword being borne for the protection of the innocent. WLC Q135 likewise names, among the duties of the sixth commandment, compliance "with all just and lawful endeavors of others, for the preservation of men's lives."

There is no vengeance in a battered woman petitioning a court to restrain her attacker. She is doing exactly what the Confession says magistrates exist to do, and submitting to the very office the Confession calls "the minister of God to thee for good."

**3. "Turning the other cheek" is not a warrant to absorb assault.**

The same catechism that requires patience and quietness of spirit (WLC Q135: "patient bearing of the hand of God, quietness of spirit") also requires "just defense thereof against violence." Patience in the Standards is the disposition that entrusts vengeance to God and refuses personal retaliation; it is not the disposition that hands one's children to a violent man. To tell an abused wife that leaving is vengeance or that protecting her children is failure to "turn the other cheek" is to wrench a passage about non-retaliation into a license for abuse.

**4. She has not "given up on the marriage"; she has not dissolved the bond.**

This is the point her accusers are most confused about. WCF 24.6 reads in full: "Nothing but adultery, or such willful desertion as can in no way be remedied by the church or civil magistrate, is cause sufficient to dissolve the bond of marriage: wherein a public and orderly course of proceeding is to be observed; and the parties concerned are not to be left to their own wills and discretion in their own case, but to be guided by the judgment of the church, to whose spiritual care and counsel they do belong, or of such as may be appointed by the church for that purpose."

Notice what this says and does not say. The Confession restricts *dissolution of the bond*. It does not require a wife to cohabit with a man who is beating her; it does not forbid physical separation as an interim measure while the church and the magistrate work; and it does not forbid the magistrate from restraining him in the meantime. Separation for safety and dissolution of the bond are two different things, and conflating them is what is actually doing violence to the Confession.

Also worth noting honestly: the husband is the one presently breaking the marriage covenant. WCF 24 describes marriage as instituted for the "mutual help and comfort" of husband and wife. A man who beats his wife and threatens his children has already abandoned the substance of his vows, even if he has not technically left the house. The church's task here is not to scold the woman for fleeing; it is to pursue the man for his sin (WCF 30), and to do so without further endangering her.

**5. What I would actually say to her and to the upset members.**

To her: You have done what the sixth commandment requires. You have used the lawful means of preservation for yourself and your children, and you have called upon the magistrate as God's minister for good. The bond of marriage is not in your hands to break, and you have not broken it. You may continue to hope for true repentance in your husband, and the church should pray and labor for that; but you do not owe him your body or your children's bodies in the meantime.

To the upset members: The pastor has not weakened marriage. He has not licensed divorce. He has distinguished between two things the Bible distinguishes — protecting the innocent and dissolving a covenant — and he has done so using the very language of the Confession and Catechisms. The charge that he is "bending Scripture to make her feel okay" is itself a bending of Scripture, for it requires her to be more "patient" than the sixth commandment requires her to be, and it treats the magistrate's sword as illegitimate. That is not fidelity to the Westminster Standards; it is a counsel of danger dressed up as a counsel of holiness.

The pastor should press on, and the session should back him — while also making sure that church discipline is now being pursued against the husband with the same seriousness they are directing at his wife.

The answer to "have I?" is, plainly, **yes**. Your wife has read the situation more faithfully than your men's group has. What you are doing is not piety; it is a compound of three or four distinct errors that the Westminster Standards name by name. Let me lay them out so you can weigh the diagnosis yourself.

---

**1. You have constructed a works-merit framework and put God in your debt.**

WCF 16.5: *"We cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin, or eternal life, at the hand of God, because of the infinite disproportion that is between us and God, and the great disproportion that is between our works and his glory, and for that they are not performed as we ought to do them; and because, when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty, and are unprofitable servants…"*

Your "claim it" formula — *I delight, I serve, I tithe, therefore He owes me the lake property* — is the precise thing the Confession denies. And WCF 16.4 makes it worse: *"no mere man, since the fall, is able perfectly to keep the commandments of God, but doth daily break them in thought, word, and deed."* So your performances are doubly insufficient — first, because fallen obedience cannot obligate the infinite God, and second, because your fallen obedience is not even perfect. The very rehearsal of your works ("I do — I'm in the Word daily, I serve, I tithe") is the rhetoric of a man who has begun to think he is paying a wage.

**2. You have read a covenant promise as a transactional receipt.**

WCF 7.1: *"The distance between God and the creature is so great, that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward, but by some voluntary condescension on God's part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant."*

The promises of God are covenantal, not contractual. The Ten Commandments' preface — *"I am the LORD thy God"* — frames every promise by His prior claim on you, not yours on Him. Psalm 37:4 is a promise about the reordering of your desires under the covenant of grace, not a slot-machine lever. WCF 1.9 likewise: *"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself: and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture… it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly."* Other places — like the tenth commandment, the chapters on providence, and the chapter on faith — speak more clearly than you have allowed.

**3. You have substituted assurance of a lake property for the assurance the Confession actually describes.**

WCF 18.1: *"Although hypocrites and other unregenerate men may vainly deceive themselves with false hopes and carnal presumptions of being in the favor of God and estate of salvation, which hope of theirs shall perish…"*

The Standards teach believers to seek assurance of being in a state of grace. They never teach assurance of particular material outcomes. Your confidence about the lake property is the very *"false hopes and carnal presumptions"* the Confession warns about, applied to a different object. If the Confession calls that kind of presumption about salvation a hope which shall perish, it has nothing better to say about presumption about a piece of real estate. You are, in fact, more confident about a lakeside purchase than the Confession permits a justified saint to be confident about his own salvation.

**4. You have denied, in practice, the providence you profess.**

WLC Q18: *"God's works of providence are his most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures, and all their actions."*

WCF 5.1: *"God the great Creator of all things does uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence…"*

Your neighbor's refusal is not, as you have come to feel, an obstacle standing between you and God's will. It is itself within God's most holy, wise, and powerful governance. To resent your neighbor is to quarrel with the providence that orders his "no" — which is to say, to quarrel with God. The first lesson of providence is that the hand you are biting is the hand that feeds you.

**5. You are in active violation of the tenth commandment.**

WSC Q81: *"The tenth commandment forbiddeth all discontentment with our own estate, envying or grieving at the good of our neighbor, and all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his."*

WLC Q109: *"The sins forbidden in the tenth commandment are, discontentment with our own estate; envying and grieving at the good of our neighbor, together with all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his."*

The lake property is, for now, your neighbor's. The resentment you have caught yourself in is the very thing the Shorter Catechism names. This is not a minor slip; it is a confessed, named sin against the last and most inward of the commandments — the one the Standards place at the end precisely because it deals with the heart.

**6. The duty you owe is precisely the one you are now failing.**

WLC Q110: *"The duties required in the tenth commandment are, such a full contentment with our own estate, in what condition soever it is, that we neither envy, nor grieve at, our neighbor's, **nor desire any thing that God sees not fit to give us**; but rejoice in what God hath given us; and study to do him all the good offices we can, and to behave ourselves toward him, and all that is his, as becometh the love of God, and the brotherhood which is between us and him."*

WSC Q80: *"The tenth commandment requireth full contentment with our own estate, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbor, and all that is his."*

Note the clause in WLC Q110: *"nor desire any thing that God sees not fit to give us."* That clause alone settles the case. Whatever the meaning of Psalm 37:4, it cannot mean that God is obligated to give you a thing He has not seen fit to give you, when the Larger Catechism's own expansion of His law says so plainly that we are not to desire any such thing.

**7. Your faith has slipped its proper object.**

WCF 14.2: *"By this faith, a Christian believeth to be true whatsoever is revealed in the word… yielding obedience to the commands, trembling at the threatenings, and embracing the promises of God for this life, and that which is to come. **But the principal acts of saving faith are accepting, receiving, and resting upon Christ alone for justification, sanctification, and eternal life, by virtue of the covenant of grace.**"*

WSC Q74: *"Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel."*

Faith rests on Christ for salvation. What you have constructed is a "faith" that rests on a formula about a lake property. That is not the faith of the Standards; it is the parody the Standards' opponents have always held up to discredit the doctrine. Take the Confession's own definition as the corrective.

**8. Your chief end has been displaced.**

WSC Q1: *"Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever."*

If the lake property has become the thing your heart chiefly wants, and God's will the obstacle to it, your chief end is no longer the chief end.

---

**The right reading of Psalm 37:4**

Read the verse whole: *"Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart."* The promise is that the desires of a heart that delights in the Lord are themselves gifts — *given*, not *possessed*. WCF 13 teaches that the Spirit works in the regenerate to bring the will into conformity with God's will, so that one no longer lusts against one's neighbor, but instead *"study[s] to do him all the good offices we can"* (WLC Q110). The lake property may come, or it may not; but a heart that has truly learned to delight in the Lord will not be able to call the neighbor's "no" a thing to resent. The psalm's promise is to that person — not to the man who has turned it into a purchase order.

---

**What to do, practically**

1. **Stop the financial moves.** WLC Q142 requires *"providential care in the management"* of what is committed to your trust. You are not exercising such care when you are staking your household's finances on a presumed answer to a presumed promise. Roll them back or pause them; consult your wife and a faithful brother.

2. **Confess the resentment** — to the Lord, and to your neighbor, as far as it can be done without hypocrisy. The tenth commandment is broken inwardly; repentance must be inward too.

3. **Repudiate the "claim it" framework publicly**, or at least among your men. WCF 1.6: *"The whole counsel of God… is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men."* Reading Psalm 37:4 as a transactional purchase order is contrary to the analogy of faith, and the men who taught it to you are not safe teachers.

4. **Re-read the Larger Catechism's exposition of the tenth commandment and the Confession's chapters on Providence (WCF 5), Saving Faith (WCF 14), and Assurance (WCF 18).** Do this with at least one older, wiser believer, and ask him to mark you.

5. **Settle the question of the lake property with this question**: *Is my heart in a posture where, if the neighbor sells to someone else and God never gives it to me, I can honestly say I delight in the Lord and the desire of my heart is Him?* If not, the desire is not yet the kind the psalm promises.

---

Your wife is right. The men who taught you this have been feeding you, and you have been feeding yourself, a doctrine of devils dressed in Bible verses. But do not despair: the work the Lord has begun in you, if it is real, will produce exactly the repentance this situation demands. Don't lean on your delight, your service, or your tithing as a credit; lean on Christ alone, who is the ground of every accepted work. Psalm 37:4 is not a contract. The covenant of grace is not a vending machine. And the tenth commandment has just been broken — which is the very thing the Shorter Catechism calls you to confess, so that, being pardoned through Christ's blood, you may *"rejoice in what God hath given us; and study to do him all the good offices we can."*

The David argument is rhetorically strong and theologically wrong, and the Westminster Standards do not back you up here. They back your elders. Let me show you why, and then give you the counsel I think you actually need.

**1. You are using a king where the Confession requires a church officer.**

David's throne was a civil/theocratic office under the old covenant, not a New Testament worship-leader's role in the church. WCF 30.1 draws this line with care: *"The Lord Jesus, as King and Head of His Church, hath therein appointed a government in the hand of Church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate."* The Standards make that distinction deliberately, and using an Israelite king to override the discipline of a New Testament officer is the precise category error 30.1 exists to prevent.

**2. Even David was not left unrestricted. Scripture says so.**

You are skipping the second half of the David story. Nathan confronted him. The child died. *"The sword shall never depart from thine house"* (2 Sam 12:10). Absalom. Sheba. Tamar. And Nathan's own word in 2 Sam 12:14: *"by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme."* The divine commendation in 1 Kings 15:5 even includes the explicit exception: *"except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite."* Scripture itself does not give David the vindication you are claiming for yourself.

And note — "man after God's own heart" (1 Sam 13:14; Acts 13:22) is a covenantal description of David's posture toward God, not a permanent exemption from consequence. Read the psalms he wrote *after* Bathsheba — 32, 38, 51, 130 — and you will see a man who wrote under the rod, not a man leading worship in protest against discipline.

**3. The Confession explicitly authorizes what your elders are doing.**

This is where your argument actually meets the text you claim to honor.

WCF 30.2: *"To these officers the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed; by virtue whereof, they have power respectively to retain and remit sins, to shut that kingdom against the impenitent, both by the Word and censures; and to open it unto the penitent, by the ministry of the gospel, and by absolution from censures, as occasion shall require."*

WCF 30.4: *"For the better attaining of these ends, the officers of the Church are to proceed by admonition, suspension from the sacrament of the Lord's Supper for a season, and excommunication from the Church; according to the nature of the crime, and demerit of the person."*

And the chapter expressly applies this to *officers*. Suspension from office is recognized in the Westminster Standards as the heavier censure appropriate to a scandalous offense by one who holds office — inflicted by the same process, for the same purpose, with the same season-of-evidence requirement. Your elders are not innovating. They are walking the road the Confession already built.

WCF 30.3 tells you the very reason this is happening to you, and it is not hostile: *"Church censures are necessary for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren, for deterring of others from the like offenses, for purging out of that leaven which might infect the whole lump, for vindicating the honor of Christ, and the holy profession of the gospel..."* The list starts with *reclaiming* — you are the first item.

**4. "Restoration means restoration" is a misreading.**

In WCF 30.4 the suspension is defined as *"a ceasing from the use thereof, until the offender give evidence of repentance."* That "until" is doing real work. Suspension *is* the form restoration takes while evidence of repentance is being gathered and displayed before the body. Your repentance — confession to your wife, confession to your pastor, counseling — is precisely what opens the door to eventual restoration. It does not, however, jump the church's discipline. The Confession refuses to let any officer privatize his repentance in a way that exempts him from the visible process.

**5. "Half the Psalter is his" cuts the other way.**

If David wrote half the Psalter, then half the Psalter is the songbook of a chastened, suspended, *silenced-from-familiarity* leader who learned to sing *"Create in me a clean heart, O God"* under God's hand. That is the David you should be citing in your own defense — and that David submits.

**My counsel.**

Stop arguing from David. Submit to your elders. The genuine repentance you describe is good; do not undo it now by treating WCF 30 as something you get to opt out of when you have a proof-text in hand.

Your elders hold the keys WCF 30 commits to them. Your repentance is what makes the door to restoration open, and the door's lock is the season of suspension the Standards describe. A man who argues his way back to the platform by appeal to a king who never held that office has not yet finished repenting.

Take the season. Honor the process. Let the congregation see the fruit — and in time, through the same authority that now suspends you, restoration will come.

No. You are not sinning against the church by calling the police. On the strongest reading of the Westminster Standards, you would be sinning if you did not. The elders' argument from 1 Corinthians 6 and Matthew 18 misapplies both passages and inverts their force. Here is the Standards-grounded case.

## 1. The civil magistrate is God's ordained avenger of evildoers, and you have a positive duty to engage his help.

**WCF 23.1:** "God, the supreme Lord and King of all the world, hath ordained civil magistrates to be, under him, over the people, for his own glory, and the public good: wherefore, in all lawful obedience to them, he hath given them the sword for the punishment of evildoers, and for the protection of them that do good."

**WCF 23.2:** "It is lawful for Christians to accept and execute the office of a magistrate… and that in the administration of his office, the magistrate may use the civil sword, for the suppression of all capital and other crimes against the civil peace, and for the protection and encouragement of them that do good."

Sexual abuse of a 15-year-old by a ministry volunteer is exactly the sort of crime these sentences describe. The magistrate is not the "unjust" party Paul objects to in 1 Corinthians 6; he is the minister of God to whom Romans 13:1–7 commits the sword.

**WLC Q191** makes engagement of that office a *positive duty* of Christians, including "employing their lawful help and assistance in the preservation of the true religion and liberties of mankind." The bodily liberty and integrity of a child in your youth ministry is precisely a "liberty of mankind" to be preserved.

## 2. The sixth commandment obligates you to protect her, including by drawing on outside help.

**WLC Q135:** "The duties required in the sixth commandment are, all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves and others by resisting all thoughts and purposes, subverting all practices, and avoiding all occasions, temptations, and practices, which tend to the unjust taking away the life of any; by just defense thereof against violence… and merciful engaging of the help of others in the preservation of the life of ourselves and others, according to the ability which God hath given us."

**WSC Q68:** "The sixth commandment requireth all lawful endeavors to preserve our own life, and the life of others."

The decisive phrase is **"merciful engaging of the help of others."** You are in fact one of the "others" the civil authority is meant to engage. To suppress the report is exactly what **WLC Q136** and **WSC Q69** forbid: "the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preservation of life." The man has already taken active steps to conceal his predation — the deletion-promise is itself consciousness of guilt. Your call is the lawful defense WLC Q135 names.

## 3. The elders' two proof-texts do not bear the weight they're being made to bear.

**(a) 1 Corinthians 6:1–7.** Read in context, Paul addresses *voluntary disputes between believers about property and money* — matters amenable to arbitration. He rebukes running to pagan courts when saints could judge. He does not address crimes against persons, least of all offenses against children. By the same pen, in Romans 13:1–7, he commands subjection to the very magistrate he elsewhere names as God's servant who "beareth not the sword in vain." The Standards receive both. **WCF 23.2** explicitly authorizes "the civil sword, for the suppression of all capital and other crimes against the civil peace." The elders cannot cite 1 Corinthians 6 against WCF 23; the Confession itself demonstrates the correct reading: that passage is about forum preference in arbitrable private disputes, not concealment of crimes.

Furthermore, this offender is not a "brother" in the relevant Matthewan sense. He has already deceived, has targeted a child (not an equal, not a "one another"), and is a continuing threat. Predatory conduct that violates the safety of the commonwealth belongs to the magistrate. To treat it as a private, arbitrable grievance is to confuse categories the Confession keeps distinct.

**(b) Matthew 18:15–17.** This passage presumes (i) a brother who has sinned against a brother, (ii) a discrete offense capable of repentance and restoration, (iii) without continuing danger to others. None of those hold here. The man acted against a child, concealed the conduct, is a likely recidivist threat to other minors in your ministry, and your "private" confrontation would expose her to retaliation while leaving every other child unprotected.

**WCF 30.2** lists church censures — "admonition, suspension from the communion of the Lord's Supper for a season, and excommunication." These are *spiritual* remedies. They cannot restrain a predator, cannot keep him away from other children, and cannot bring him under the State's incapacitating power. **WCF 30.4** directs officers to proceed "according to the nature of the offense" — and the nature of this offense is that it is *criminal, predatory, and ongoing*. The Confession nowhere grants the church the civil sword; it operates strictly in its own sphere.

## 4. The "dirty laundry" argument is precisely inverted.

Hiding a confessed sexual abuser from the State does not honor Christ; it uses His name as a shield for predation, endangers other children he may approach, and signals to victims that the church values its reputation above their safety. The Standards' language is plain: the magistrate exists for "the punishment of evildoers, and for the protection of them that do good" (WCF 23.1). Cooperating with that protection is the faithful thing. Concealment is the scandal; disclosure is the faithfulness.

## 5. What to do.

1. **Call the police now.** You are obeying WCF 23 and WLC Q135. Document what she told you with the specific details that make her account credible; preserve any texts, timestamps, or other records she still has. The deletion-promise is itself evidence of consciousness of guilt. Most jurisdictions also impose a *legal* duty to report — and WCF 23 frames such laws as lawful obedience owed.

2. **Do not treat the elders' instruction as binding on this point.** They have misapplied Scripture and the Standards. Their proposed course — private confrontation of a concealed predator and "restoration if he repents" — fails to protect her, fails to protect the other children in your ministry, and exceeds the church's lawful sphere (WCF 30).

3. **Seek counsel from a faithful Christian outside this session** — a confessional Reformed pastor or another session's leadership. The local elders have disqualified themselves on this matter. This is not schism; it is the prudence the Confession assumes in WCF 30–31.

4. **If you face pressure to retract or to be silent,** remember that silence now may make you complicit if another child is harmed. WLC Q135's "just defense thereof against violence" covers this; WLC Q192 forbids "withdrawing that assistance which they [magistrates] require" by lawful means.

The shortest version: **WCF 23 gives the magistrate the sword for crimes exactly like this; WLC Q135 commands merciful engagement of outside help, including the State, to preserve the bodily integrity of the vulnerable; WCF 30 nowhere gives the church the civil sword.** The elders' reading of 1 Corinthians 6 and Matthew 18 cannot stand against those texts. Your instinct is informed conscience. Call the police.

Your teacher's counsel is mistaken, and the Westminster Standards are unusually pointed about this — they treat the very chapter he is preaching from as teaching the *opposite* of what he is drawing out of it. Walk through this with me.

**1. The misreading the Standards will not sustain.**

The passage in your teacher's mouth — "money is the root of all evil" — is not what the text says. The KJV itself has "the *love* of money is the root of all evil" (1 Tim. 6:10). That single word is the hinge. The Larger Catechism, expounding the tenth commandment, gives the authoritative reading:

> "The sins forbidden in the tenth commandment are, such as these: discontentment with our own estate; ... **over-loving, and inordinate setting of the heart upon any of our good things, and immoderate joy therein; inordinate desires of, or inordinate use of, or inordinate delight in any of our lawful good things**; immoderate and worldly sorrow; trusting in lawful good things for happiness; setting the heart on present good things to the neglect of things above; taking up our rest in them; taking unlawful and undue courses for their increase and preservation..." (WLC Q110)

Note the word that does all the work: *inordinate*. Possession, use, and delight in lawful goods are not the target — *inordinate* possession, use, and delight are. The proof-texts WLC Q110 assembles for this very question include 1 Timothy 6. So the chapter is not teaching your teacher what he says it teaches; the chapter is teaching what the Standards say it teaches, which is the opposite of liquidation.

**2. The Standards positively require what he calls sin.**

This is the centerpiece. The eighth commandment — "thou shalt not steal" — is the place where Scripture lays out the Christian's positive duties with money. WLC Q108 is explicit:

> "The duties required in the eighth commandment are, truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; rendering to every one his due; restitution of goods unlawfully detained from the owners; giving and lending freely, according to our ability, and the necessities of others; **moderation in our own countenance, procurements, and employments; and a provident care in the managing of our affairs, that we may be able both to relieve the needy, and to leave others a competent portion after us**." (WLC Q108)

The proof-text behind the last clause is, among others, 1 Timothy 6:6–8 — the verses immediately before your teacher's text. Three things to mark in that sentence:

- *"Provident care in the managing of our affairs"* — running an HVAC company with foresight is a *required* Christian duty, not a tolerable compromise.
- *"Able to relieve the needy"* — charity is commanded, but it is *funded by*, not undone by, the prudently-managed estate.
- *"Leave others a competent portion after us"* — leaving an inheritance to your wife and three children is named, by name, as a Christian duty.

That last phrase is aimed straight at you. You are not free, on this Confession, to call the eighth commandment's required provision "the root of all evil." The Standards will not let you.

**3. The rich young ruler and "lay not up for yourselves."**

Two points here.

First, the rich young ruler was a specific word to a specific man, with a specific idol. The Confession carefully distinguishes the abiding moral law (which "doth for ever bind all," WCF 19.5) from particular gospel calls that the law's general equity does not universalize. WCF 19.4 explicitly removes the Jewish judicial laws from present obligation "further than the general equity thereof may require." By the same token, Christ's "sell all that thou hast" to that young man is not a standing command on every prospering tradesman with a father-in-law's bequest.

Second, this is exactly the situation the Confession addresses in the chapter on Christian liberty:

> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in any thing, contrary to His Word; or beside it, in matters of faith and worship. So that, to require such things to be believed and received, or to require them as terms of Christian communion, that are not so made by God in his Word, is to invade the prerogative of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the sole lawgiver and king in his church..." (WCF 20.2)

Your teacher has told you "the spiritual move is clear." That is the formulation the Confession is written to resist. Nothing in Scripture binds your conscience to liquidate the business and dump the inheritance; a man who tells you otherwise is binding where God has not bound.

As for Matthew 6:19–21, the Standards read it as a heart-direction, not a hand-direction. The fourth petition of the Lord's Prayer, "give us this day our daily bread," explicitly asks God to keep on giving bread that we may then receive and enjoy with thankfulness — which presupposes an ordinary means of provision that includes your labor and your capital (WLC Q144). "Lay not up" is rebuked as an inordinate *setting of the heart* on the deposit, not as a prohibition on the deposit itself.

**4. Your fatherly duty under the fifth commandment.**

WLC Q139 makes your situation concrete:

> "The duties of superiors are, to pray for and bless those under their charge; to instruct, counsel, and admonish them; countenancing, comforting, and protecting them; **providing for them things needful for soul and body**; and a prudent and exemplary carriage, that the blessing of God may be upon them."

"Things needful for soul and body" plainly covers more than this month's take-home. It includes an education fund, a cushion against the slow years every HVAC business has, working capital in the company that pays the wages, and the inheritance your eighth-commandment duty says you are to leave "after you." A father who dismantles all of that on a teacher's intuition is not walking by faith; he is failing the fifth commandment's provision requirement while imagining he is fulfilling the eighth's charity requirement.

**5. Your wife.**

Listen to her. WCF 24.2 grounds the marriage bond in the wife's being given as a "mutual help meet" to the husband — your providential help, not a hindrance to be overruled. WLC Q138–Q139 lays on the family head the duty of "prudent and exemplary carriage," which is incompatible with steamrolling a wife who can see that the proposed course would gut the very business that feeds the children. And WLC Q110, on the tenth commandment's forbiddances, expressly names "discontentment with our own estate" as sin — which, in your case, has been manufactured by a teacher into contempt for your own lawful, providential condition. Your wife's counsel is part of how God is keeping you from that.

**6. What I would actually tell you to do.**

- *Keep the business. Run it as stewardship.* WLC Q108 is your charter: faithful contracts, just wages, provident management, leaving a competent portion after you. A good year is not a sin to be undone; it is a trust to be administered.
- *Give generously, liberally, now* — from both the business profits and the inheritance, to the church, to the needy, to gospel causes. The eighth commandment's charity duty is real and grows with what God entrusts to you. But "give it all now" is not the same as "give generously now," and the Standards distinguish them.
- *Cultivate the contentment the Standards actually call for*: "full contentment with our own condition" (WLC Q109). That is a heart-work, not a balance-sheet work. The opposite of the love of money is not the liquidation of money; it is contentment with God, liberality with what you have, and faithful stewardship of what is in your hands.
- *Test the inner turmoil.* Conviction comes from God's Word applied in season; it does not contradict the same Word's plain duties. When a teacher's "spiritual move" makes you want to disobey WLC Q108, Q139, and WCF 24 at the same time, the discomfort you are feeling is not the Spirit's witness against your provision — it is the friction of an imposed conscience (WCF 20.2) against the actual shape of obedience.
- *Be glad.* Thank God for the inheritance, the business, the wife, the three children, the year of grace. Hold goods loosely in your heart and firmly in your hands for their proper uses.

The Standards, reading the same chapter your teacher reads, put a faithful provider, a generous giver, and a content heart in the same paragraph — and they never put a liquidation in any of them.

**No. Refilling the prescription is not a forfeiture of healing, and stopping it is not an act of faith. What you have been taught is not the gospel, and the Westminster Standards address each of its errors specifically.**

I will go through the layers of the claim, citing the Standards.

---

**1. The claim is built on a wrong doctrine of faith.**

Saving faith is not the assertion of an isolated promise. The Confession defines it this way:

> "By this faith, a Christian believeth to be true whatsoever is revealed in the Word, for the authority of God himself speaking therein; and acteth differently upon that which each particular passage thereof containeth; **yielding obedience to the commands, trembling at the threatenings, and embracing the promises of God for this life and that which is to come.**" (WCF 14.2)

Notice the threefold act. Faith embraces promises, but it also obeys commands and trembles at threatenings. The teaching you received has amputated "embracing the promises" from "obeying the commands" and built a system where one Scripture overrides another. James 5:15 and 1 Peter 2:24 are real, but so is the sixth commandment's command to preserve your life, and so is the wisdom of God revealed in the means of preservation. Faith receives the whole counsel.

**2. The teaching confuses faith with presumption, and offers a false assurance.**

The Confession is explicit:

> "This infallible assurance doth not so belong to the spirit of adoption, as that **a true believer may, without singular revelation, attain thereunto**..." (WCF 18.3)

What your healing ministry gave you is exactly what the Confession warns against: a "singular revelation" of personal health claims, presented as though it were a work of the Spirit, used to override ordinary duties. The Confession says true assurance "in the diligent use of means" is what believers may attain (WCF 18.3). Throwing away the bottle is the opposite of diligent use of means. The wave of guilt you feel is not the conviction of the Spirit; it is the voice of a system that has placed you under law, telling you that your bodily safety depends on the strength of your faith. The Spirit does not require you to stop taking your medicine in order to prove your trust in Christ.

**3. The verses you were given are being read out of context.**

On **1 Peter 2:24** — "by whose stripes ye were healed." The Standards read this in its context, which is spiritual. WSC 85 says Christ executes His priestly office "in his once offering himself a sacrifice without spot to God, **to be a reconciliation for the sins of the people**, and in making continual intercession for them." The "healing" in 1 Peter 2:24 is bound to the preceding clause: "that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness." The stripe-bearing of Christ is the ground of our justification and sanctification, not a deposit slip redeemable for physical health on demand. The Shorter Catechism's framing (Q86–88) makes this clear: the benefits of Christ's death are "redemption from the curse of the law," "reconciliation with God," and the like. To make this passage a guarantee of epilepsy-free physiology is to wrench it from the gospel.

On **James 5:14–15** — the prayer of faith. This is real. But it sits within a passage that itself assumes the ordinary means of God's care: calling the elders, anointing with oil, confession of sins, mutual prayer. The Standards do not turn this into a mechanical "bad confession" gauge, and neither does the text. WCF 21.1 forbids worship that is "devised" by man beyond what the Word has instituted: "*it is not lawful for any man to devise, or follow any other way.*" The "point of contact" ritual of throwing out the bottle is an invented worship, not a commanded one.

**4. You are under a duty to preserve your life, and your conscience is being mis-trained against that duty.**

> "The sins forbidden in the sixth commandment are, all taking away the life of ourselves or of others... **the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preservation of life**..." (WSC Q68)

A daily antiepileptic is, by all ordinary evidence, a lawful and necessary means of preservation of life for you. To withdraw it on the authority of a private "revelation" is precisely what this Catechism names as sin. It is also, considered as a vow, void before God:

> "No man may vow to do anything... **that hinders any duty therein commanded**, or that is not in his own power, and for the performance whereof he hath no promise from God. In which respects... [such vows] are so far from being degrees of higher perfection, that they are superstitious and sinful snares, in which no Christian may entangle himself." (WCF 22.7)

The implicit vow you made — "I will not take this medicine as a confession of faith" — hinders a duty that God has commanded (preservation of life) and rests on a "promise" (automatic physical healing in this life) that the Westminster Standards do not recognize and the cited verses do not teach. The Confession calls such a vow a *superstitious and sinful snare*.

**5. The providence of God works through second causes.**

> "Although, in relation to the foreknowledge and decree of God, the first Cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly; so that nothing happens to any person or thing, against his will, or without his appointment: **yet, by the same providence, he ordereth them to fall out, according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently.**" (WCF 5.2)

Antiepileptic medication is, in the ordinary providence of God, a second cause He uses to preserve your life. The God who ordained your days also ordained the means. To throw away the means in order to test the God of the means is not faith; it is the trial of Christ, rebuked in Scripture. Faith uses the means God has given; it does not jettison them in pursuit of a higher experience.

---

**What to do, then.**

First, take the medicine. This is obedience. The auras you have had are warnings, both medically and theologically — they are signs that your present course is destroying what God has given you to protect.

Second, lay down the guilt. The guilt you feel when you consider refilling the prescription is a manufactured conscience, not a Christian one. WCF 14.2 describes a faith that *embraces* the promises and *yields obedience* to the commands; the system you have been taught sets these two against each other. The Christian conscience that the Spirit produces will tell you that to love your wife (whose terror is itself a calling to repentance) and to keep your body for her and for your neighbor (Epi 5:28) is part of holiness, not a violation of it.

Third, examine the ministry. The teaching adds to God's Word a promise He has not made, replaces the ordinary means of providence with a ritual, and produces a fruits that the Confession's chapter on assurance (WCF 18) explicitly distinguishes from the work of the Spirit. Do not let their framework continue to interpret your conscience.

Fourth, take this to your own pastor or session. This is not a private matter; it concerns your life, your wife's life with you, and the doctrine of the church. WCF 31 speaks of synods and councils; WCF 30 of church government. Walking this out alone, under the authority of a single teacher, is part of how the snare closed on you.

---

You asked whether taking the medication is a failure of faith. According to the Standards of the church catholic and reformed, **failing to take it is the failure**. The Confession's chapter on providence (5.2), the Catechism's exposition of the sixth commandment (WSC Q68), the chapter on vows (WCF 22.7), and the definition of saving faith itself (WCF 14.2) all converge on the same answer: refill the bottle, repent of the framework that told you to throw it out, and let your faith obey the whole God — the God of the promise and of the pill, the God of grace and of second causes, who "worketh all things after the counsel of his own will" (WCF 2.2) precisely by working through the means He has appointed.

Friend,

I want to honor the sincerity behind this. You are trying to take Paul seriously, and you have a real appetite for devotion. The trouble is that in reaching for the "more spiritual" path, you have set yourselves against an ordinance of God, and the Westminster Standards let us see this clearly. Let me lay out the fourfold problem with what you've done, and then what I would urge in response.

**1. You have read Paul against Paul. Scripture must interpret Scripture.**

WCF 1.9: *"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself: therefore, when there arises a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly."*

The very chapter you cite contains Paul's own instruction that directly forbids your arrangement. 1 Corinthians 7:5 — sitting in the middle of the verses you've quoted: *"Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control."*

When a verse seems to commend a high view of singleness, the very next relevant text in the same letter tells married believers not to impose singleness on one another. The Westminster hermeneutic sends us to read the more ambiguous by the more clear — not the other way around. The "higher" calling Paul commends (1 Cor 7:7) is singleness for those *to whom God has given the gift*, not a self-imposed celibacy inside an existing marriage. And even the narrow exception Paul allows (a season of abstinence by mutual consent for prayer, followed by reunion) explicitly rules out what you have now done for six weeks.

**2. Marriage is a divine ordinance whose purposes you cannot redesign.**

WCF 24.2: *"Marriage was ordained for the mutual help of husband and wife; for the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue, and of the church with an holy seed; and for the prevention of uncleanness."*

Three God-appointed ends are named: mutual help, holy offspring, and the prevention of uncleanness. By your own decision you have undermined two of them — the mutual help that includes the conjugal bond, and the prevention of uncleanness (cf. 1 Cor 7:2, *"because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife"*). Marriage is not a lifestyle you are free to remodel as your spiritual preferences evolve; it is a divine ordinance with ends God has fixed. A husband has authority within marriage; he does not have authority to redesign the marriage bed out of existence.

**3. The seventh commandment positively requires conjugal duty.**

WLC Q139 lists among the duties required by the seventh commandment *"conjugal love and duty"* and *"the preservation of the marriage bed undefiled."* WLC Q138 names among the sins forbidden the neglect of any of these duties. This is not merely a prohibition on adultery; it is a positive charge to render what 1 Corinthians 7:3 calls "due benevolence," and to keep the bed undefiled (Heb 13:4).

What you are doing is the *opposite* of both. Withholding the conjugal bond indefinitely, without scriptural warrant, is not "undefiled preserving" — it is the neglect of a duty the Standards explicitly require. And this is the more serious because, in the order of your home, you are the one withholding what is owed.

**4. You are courting exactly the danger Paul warns of.**

Paul's stated reason for commanding reunion after a season of prayer is striking: *"so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control."* The Westminster view of human nature — that we are corrupt and prone to break out into the very uncleanness marriage is meant to prevent — fits this warning exactly. You have removed the God-appointed means of preservation; the temptation that means was given to prevent is now knocking, in at least one of your hearts. Do not be surprised, and do not pretend the warning is hypothetical.

**5. "Mostly on board" is itself a red flag.**

Even the narrow exception Paul permits requires *mutual* consent and is for *a time*, with explicit reunion built in. A spouse who is anything less than fully persuaded removes you from even the Bible's allowance. And a "season" is not a permanent restructuring of the marriage.

---

**What I urge you to do.**

1. **Stop.** Same bed, full conjugal life restored. The arrangement has been wrong from the start, and continuing it compounds the sin.
2. **Repent together.** Confess this to God and to one another. Your motive was not malice, but it was a real fault against a divine ordinance and a real wrong toward your wife. Christ covers it; do not leave it uncovered.
3. **Pursue prayer and fasting as the Bible actually models — together.** Prayer is not opposed to the marriage bed; the marriage bed, kept undefiled, is itself part of your sanctification. There is no "higher" path that cuts against the ordinance God gave you.
4. **If you believe God has given one or both of you the gift of singleness**, that calling is exercised by being unmarried, not by reinventing marriage. The Standards teach that this gift is given to few (cf. 1 Cor 7:7), and that for most the calling is marriage lived faithfully as a covenant.
5. **Bring this to your pastor or eldership**, and accept their counsel. A decision this weighty should not be carried privately.

**Counsel:**

You're not facing a tie-breaker between two equal goods. You're facing a direct collision between an explicit divine command and a strong temporal preference, and the Westminster Standards are not ambiguous about how to weigh that.

**On the Sabbath itself.** The Confession (21.7-8) and Shorter Catechism (Q. 60) require that the whole Sabbath day be spent in public and private worship, with rest even from "such worldly employments and **recreations as are lawful on other days**." Note the precision: the Standards don't just forbid evil recreations; they forbid *lawful* ones, because the Sabbath's design is a different kind of rest than ordinary days. An elite Sunday-morning league, eight months of the year, is exactly the category the Standards identify — recreation, lawful in itself, displaced from Sabbath observance for competitive purposes.

**On "the Sabbath was made for man."** This argument actually cuts the other way. Jesus said the Sabbath serves human good (Mk 2:27) in defense of works of *necessity and mercy* — plucking grain, healing the sick. The Confession (21.8) preserves that same exception. Recreational league play is neither necessity nor mercy. The verse affirms the *purpose* of the Sabbath (human flourishing through holy rest), not its dispensability for any preference. To deploy it as a general permission slip is to read it backwards.

**On "God cares about your heart, not your attendance."** The Confession (21.5) and Larger Catechism (Q. 108) describe the duties of the Sabbath as both inward (heart preparation, holy affections) and outward (assembling, hearing, praying). Attendance and heart are not alternatives; they are paired. Your youth pastor's framing is not the Standards' framing, and a family seeking Reformed counsel should weigh that carefully.

**On the "pipeline."** The Confession orders goods such that spiritual formation is not negotiable for temporal advancement (WCF 21; LC Q. 124-129 on parental duty to "warn them against...the profaning of the Sabbath"). Scouting windows open repeatedly across adolescence; the Sabbath principle does not. Closing one door to keep a higher duty is not cruelty — it is the ordering the Standards require of parents.

**On peer practice.** The Confession explicitly cites Exodus 23:2 against following a multitude in things evil, and Sabbath-breaking is classed as sin. Half the team being church kids doesn't change the category of the act; it only enlarges the company.

**On the "guilt-piling" reaction.** Faithful application of God's Word sometimes produces godly conviction — the very thing the third use of the law is designed to produce. That's categorically different from manipulation. If the counsel feels heavy, that is the law doing its proper work, not the counselor doing improper work.

**One sentence, as you asked:** No — don't sign him up for a league whose regular season requires Sunday-morning play; pursue his development through a club that doesn't require him to trade the means of grace for eight months of the year, and treat the "Sunday" conflict as itself a catechetical moment your eleven-year-old is old enough to begin to understand.

## What Jeremiah 29:11 Actually Says, and to Whom

The Confession is plain about how we read a contested verse. **WCF 1.9**: *"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself: and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any passage (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly."*

Jeremiah 29:11 was spoken to the exiles in Babylon — seventy years of discipline, not entrepreneurial destiny. The "expected end" (Hebrew *'acharit*) is a word the prophets use for the messianic restoration, the return from exile, and ultimately the new covenant. Read in context (Jeremiah 29:10, 12–14), it is a word about *prayer* and *return from Babylon*, not a blank check for a Series A. To wrench a national, covenantal, eschatological promise into a personal guarantee of business success is precisely the kind of interpretation that WCF 1.9 forbids — it is not "searching other places that speak more clearly." It is, frankly, **WCF 16.1** territory: *"Good works are only such as God hath commanded in his holy Word, and not such as, without the warrant thereof, are devised by men out of blind zeal, or upon any pretence of good intentions."* You have devised a "promised end" for yourself that the Word does not promise.

## What Saving Faith Actually Is

The Confession defines faith in a way that should stop you in your tracks. **WCF 14.2**: *"By this faith a Christian believeth to be true whatsoever is revealed in the Word, for the authority of God himself speaking therein; and acteth differently upon that which each particular passage thereof containeth; yielding obedience to the commands, trembling at the threatenings, and embracing the promises of God for this life, and that which is to come."*

And the Shorter Catechism says it as plainly as anything in the Standards: **WSC 86**: *"Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel."*

Note two things. (1) Faith is a *receiving and resting upon Christ for salvation*, not a positive-confession engine for business outcomes. (2) Faith believes *what is revealed in the Word*. Jeremiah 29:11 does not reveal that your startup will win. You have not been "standing on the promise" — you have been standing on a private impression, and calling the impression Scripture. Your mentor's "don't let doubt abort it" is a counsel to silence the very means God has given you to test impressions against the Word (WCF 1.9). That is dangerous.

This present collapse may be that. It is at minimum *a* thing God is doing, not a breach. A god who reneges is a god you invented. Here is the doctrinal reasoning, point by point.

---

**1. The seventh commandment forbids the heart, not only the hand.**

Your friends treat the issue as if the only thing that matters is what you did or didn't do physically. The Confession rejects that framing. WLC Q139, listing the sins forbidden by the seventh commandment, names **"all unclean imaginations, thoughts, purposes, and affections"** as forbidden. WSC Q72 says the same thing in shorter form: the seventh commandment requires **"the preservation of chastity in heart and life."**

By your own description, you were already there. Long private chats, a flirtatious running thread, and "I know exactly where it was heading in my head" — that is the precise pathology WLC Q139 has in view. Cutting it off is not a heroic measure; it is the first step of obedience to a commandment that was already being broken in your affections, regardless of your body.

**2. The commandment's scope explicitly includes the "incentives" you cut off.**

This is the most directly relevant point, and it is the one your friends are denying.

WLC Q99 sets the interpretive rule: **"under one sin or duty, all of the same kind are forbidden or commanded; together with all the causes, means, occasions, and appearances thereof, and provocations thereunto."**

WLC Q140 spells the rule out for the seventh commandment: the duty includes **"abstaining from all occasions and appearances of evil, and from all provocations to, and what may be an incentive unto, the sins forbidden in the seventh commandment."**

And WLC Q139 itself closes the catalogue of forbidden sins with **"lascivious songs, books, pictures, dancings, stage plays, and all other provocations to, or what may be an incentive unto, the sins forbidden in the seventh commandment."**

So when you moved your desk, muted the thread, and dropped the shows and accounts that fed the same appetite, you were not inventing a new rule. You were doing the thing the Larger Catechism literally calls "abstaining from all occasions and appearances of evil" and the Shorter Catechism calls **"a guard against all uncleanness … as may be incentives thereunto."** The Matthew 5:29 language and the "flee fornication" language of 1 Corinthians 6:18 are applications of this same principle, not exaggerations of it.

**3. The two friends' objections, measured against the Standards.**

*"You're being repressive and legalistic."* The Standards frame mortification of these specific sins as a *duty*, not a counsel of perfection. WLC Q75 defines sanctification as the work of grace by which we are **"enabled more and more to die unto sin, and live unto righteousness,"** and WLC Q76 defines repentance as turning from known sin **"with grief and hatred,"** not with a half-regret. There is no softer register in the seventh commandment's treatment of "unclean imaginations" or "unchaste company."

*"You have made an idol out of purity."* This conflates two different things. WSC Q47 says the first commandment requires us **"to worship and glorify [God] accordingly."** That is what the first table governs — the orientation of the heart to God. The second table, including the seventh commandment, governs our duty to our neighbor (and, in the chastity requirement, to ourselves). You weren't worshipping purity; you were practicing fidelity (WLC Q138: **"fidelity in covenants betwixt husband and wife; mutual love, confidence, and assistance"**) and protecting the chastity of your own heart. The Standards treat those as duties, not idols. Idolatry would be trusting the amputation to save you. Obedience is doing the thing because God commanded it.

*"A mature adult can just 'manage boundaries' without amputating."* Note the Confession's actual verb: not "manage" but **"abstain."** To keep a recurring private flirtation in your life, with a desk-move as the chief restraint, is to remain in the very "appearance of evil" the Catechism commands you to *abstain from*. The Standards' prescribed obedience is removal. "Managing" the proximity while continuing in it is a partial obedience the Confession does not recognize as fulfilling the commandment.

**4. A few pastoral notes, for the next steps.**

You did the right thing, but the right thing is the *beginning* of obedience, not the end. A few implications worth pressing:

- **Repent of the affection, not just of the consequences.** WLC Q76 describes repentance as grief and hatred of the sin itself. It is one thing to be relieved you didn't act on it; it is another to be horrified that the affection formed in you at all. The Standards expect the latter.

- **Go to your wife.** WLC Q138 ties fidelity to marriage as a covenant. Hiding what was in your heart from the woman you owe fidelity to is a separate sin, even if you ended the affair. Do this with a pastor or mature Christian alongside you if you are afraid the conversation will be destructive, but do it. WLC Q138 also requires **"preservation of chastity … in ourselves and others,"** and the chaste regard owed to your wife includes the candor she is owed as a covenant partner.

- **Mortification is a way of life, not a one-time act.** WLC Q75–78 frames the Christian life as a continuing work of dying and rising. Expect the same appetite to reappear in new forms; the same principles apply each time. Ordinary means — prayer, the word, the sacraments, an accountable friend — are not optional supplements to your decisive act; they are how the act is sustained.

- **Discount the friends' mockery in proportion to its source.** Their counsel is itself under the same commandment. WSC Q71 forbids **"all unchaste thoughts, words, and actions,"** and WLC Q139 forbids **"corrupt or filthy communications, or listening thereunto."** Telling a man he is repressive for cutting off a flirtation, while describing the flirtation with amusement, is not neutral advice.
