# Evaluating Three Acts of Teaching on Chastity

Using the Westminster Standards as the test.

## The governing rules

From the *Shorter Catechism* (Q/A 7–8): the end of man is to glorify God and enjoy him forever, and the means is keeping "perfect obedience" to the revealed will of God. The Confession (ch. 1 §§6, 9; ch. 2 §2; ch. 21) requires that Scripture be preached in such a manner that the *whole counsel of God* is opened, with sincerity (not in the "enticing words of man's wisdom," 1 Cor. 2:4–5, cited WCF I.9), and that worship and means of grace be "taken up with such circumstances… as are requisite to the natural end of the ordinance" (WCF 21.5). Add: WCF 10.3–4 on the Spirit's ordinary work of producing conviction, repentance, and faith through the Word itself, not through manufactured techniques of the preacher's own devising.

So on every axis the question is the same: **does this teaching actually deliver the ordained means — the Word of God opened, Christ held up, sin unmasked and the conscience turned to the living Christ?** The three axes (matter, manner, end) collapse into one: does this *serve the hearer in the way God has appointed, or has the leader inserted himself as a more reliable agent than the Spirit and the Word?*

---

## Leader A — evaluated

**Matter.** Complete. The doctrine of chastity is delivered in its positive shape (desire aimed at covenant, the body honored as created), its negative shape (sin named in all its forms, including the digital ones the culture prefers to euphemize), and its remedial shape (repentance and cleansing for the fallen). Nothing forbidden is hidden; nothing required is softened.

**Manner.** Honest and pastoral. Anonymous questions honor the conscience of the asker while refusing to let the classroom avoid hard cases. Married and single futures held together avoids the snare of treating chastity as merely a *purity-until-marriage* countdown (which flatters the married and abandons the single, and inverts the Confession's treatment of marriage as one good among others under the larger frame of serving Christ, WCF 24–25). The gospel frame — "none of you is your worst search history" — is precisely the Confession's doctrine of forgiveness through Christ applied: the filth of sin washed, the filth of self-image addressed (WCF 11.1; 15.5; S.C. Q/A 32–33, 84).

**End.** Right. The students' true good, which is the same as God's glory: that they would know the truth, believe it, and be set free from sin by Christ.

**Verdict:** Sound. This is what WCF I.9 calls for — truth revealed in Scripture opened to the conscience without addition of "the imaginations of men's hearts."

---

## Leader B — evaluated

**Matter.** Doctrinally the content is intact; the syllabus is honored. The matter of the teaching is not deficient. *The failure is not here.* Leader B has every piece of chastity teaching on the table.

**Manner.** This is where the act fails. Three specified design choices:

1. **The chewed-gum object lesson.** It teaches the doctrine of the perishable body, but it teaches it by making a real student, or a real student surrogate, into a prop. The body is being "honored" by being made an object lesson in humiliation. This conflicts with WCF 24.1 (the body as honored), but more sharply with the general moral rule of WCF 13 (the third use of the law, and the duty of love to neighbor) — using a person as a *means* to another person's moral education is exactly the form against which Scripture warns (Gal. 6:1; 1 Cor. 8:9).

2. **The signed purity pledge under parental spotlight.** This is a vow extracted from minors under institutional pressure, with parents as witnesses for enforcement. Two problems: (a) the Confession treats vow-taking with gravity (WCF 22.6–7; S.C. Q/A 113–114) — vows are not to be made rashly, and certainly not as the climactic act of a coercive assembly; (b) a vow that the minor cannot keep and was nudged to make becomes, if broken, a second wound added to the first fall. The *design* manufactures a future occasion of deeper shame — which is the opposite of what the Confession says the ministry of the Word is meant to do (WCF 10.3; 15.5; 18.4).

3. **Testimonies "selected for maximal shame-detail."** This is the worst of the three. A testimony belongs to the one who offers it; to curate testimony for *its shame-value to the audience* is to instrumentalize another person's sin for your pedagogical effect. This is explicitly forbidden by WCF 13 (the requirement of truthfulness in dealings with neighbor) and is a corruption of the Confession's doctrine of confession (WCF 15.6): confession is to be made voluntarily, with the soul's burden known to a faithful counselor, *for relief and restoration*, not for stagecraft.

**End.** The stated design note gives the game away: "so they finally get it, they need to feel the stakes in their stomach." The end has been shifted from *the student's true good (glorifying and enjoying God)* to *producing a felt sensation in the student's stomach.* That is exactly the move the Confession warns against in WCF 1.9 and WCF 10.3 — substituting the preacher's technique for the Spirit's ordinary work through the Word. The Holy Spirit produces conviction; the preacher's job is to open the text (S.C. Q/A 155–156). To engineer dread as the means of persuasion is to distrust both the text and the Spirit.

**Verdict:** Fails on **manner** and **end**. The matter is intact, but the *act* of teaching is corrupted because (a) it treats students as means, (b) it sets traps (vows, public commitment) that will become future wounds, and (c) it locates the agent of conviction in the leader's technique rather than in the Word and Spirit.

**What B got right.** The insistence that chastity is not merely *sweet* but *costly*; that sin is not merely "unwise choices" but has real consequences; that the body and its acts are not detachable from the self; that the classroom must not flinch from naming sin plainly. These are real goods. The error is in *how* the stakes are made present — through manufactured shame rather than through the unveiled Word.

---

## Leader C — evaluated

**Matter.** Defective, by silence. The Confession (WCF 1.6, 21.3, 25.2) requires that Scripture be opened to the people; the Larger Catechism (Q/A 154, 157) requires that the minister "open and apply the whole counsel of God" and "not suppress any part of the truth." C's unit does not suppress the truth by denying it; it suppresses it by renaming, omitting, and re-aiming. To rename sin "unwise choices" is not translation — it is redefinition, and it works a real loss: the very word "sin" is the one Scripture itself uses to bring conviction (S.C. Q/A 84). To omit the digital forms because they are "too awkward" is exactly to "suppress" a portion of the truth the students are facing daily — which is the *moral* matter of chastity for them, not an optional appendix.

**Manner.** Warmth is right; privacy (anonymous questions) is right. But the manner is finally in the service of the matter, and the matter has been hollowed. Warmth without the wound of truth is sentimentality, not pastoral love.

**End.** "You're loved no matter what, so make choices that feel right for you." Two errors, in one sentence:

1. **"You're loved no matter what."** Half-true and therefore false. WCF 11.1 — the Father loves the elect in Christ; but the love of God is *not* an unconditional sentiment detached from Christ and the covenant. The love C is offering is *separate from* the truth of the sin and the need of the Savior. The Confession's order is always: sin revealed, Christ revealed, *therefore* the love of God is known. Reversing this order converts the gospel into a generic benevolence that costs the hearer nothing and changes the hearer never.

2. **"Make choices that feel right for you."** This is the assertion of moral autonomy as the final authority — which the Confession explicitly denies (WCF 2.2: God alone is Lord of the conscience). The unit ends with *the student's own felt sense* as the criterion, having stripped away the law of God as the criterion. The "safe voice" becomes, in fact, the most dangerous voice, because the Confession's diagnosis is that *the heart is the deceiver* (WCF 6.2 — "the heart of man is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked"); a curriculum that hands the deceived heart back to itself as its own guide is not pastoral care.

**Verdict:** Fails on **matter** and **end**. The manner is partly right (anonymity, warmth of tone), but manner without matter is a pleasant form around an empty or false substance.

**What C got right.** Two things:

(a) The recognition that *shame is not the gospel.* The Confession never treats shame as the means of grace (WCF 10.3 — conviction is the Spirit's work, through truth, not through stagecraft). C correctly identifies that some chastity curricula are designed to humiliate the already-fallen, and refuses to add to their burden.

(b) The pastoral instinct to be a *safe place* in a culture where students are pelted with shame from every direction — peers, social media, sometimes even the church. This instinct is the same one WCF 15.6 gives: the church is to receive "such as walk according to their own lusts," and WCF 18.4 — that the minister is to deal tenderly with the tempted and fallen. C's error is not in *wanting* to be a safe voice; it is in *thinking* the safe voice's job is to *remove* truth. The Confession's safe voice keeps the truth intact *and* holds it in the love of Christ (cf. S.C. Q/A 31–33; L.C. Q/A 159).

---

## Ranking

The ranking is on the *act of teaching*, not on the sincerity of the leader (which is stipulated equal).

1. **Leader A.** Sound in matter, manner, and end. This is the act the Confession contemplates when it calls ministers to "open and apply the whole counsel of God" (L.C. Q/A 159) in sincerity (WCF 1.9) and to be "apt to teach" with "a due sense of the importance and difficulty of the work" (WCF 27.4).

2. **Leader B.** Materially complete but formally corrupted; the end has been redirected toward manufactured affect. The act as *teaching* fails; the act as *pastoral discipline* fails harder, because it sets snares (vows, public commitments) and wounds (instrumentalized testimonies).

3. **Leader C.** Materially defective; the end has been inverted (felt sense becomes the criterion) under cover of warmth. The act as *teaching* fails by omission; the act as *pastoral care* is a more complicated failure, because it preserves the symptom (kindness) while losing the substance (truth that sets free, John 8:32, WCF 19).

**The directional summary.** B and C are mirror errors, both rooted in the same displacement: both substitute *the teacher's chosen effect on the student* for *the Word's own operation through the Spirit.* B displaces by *adding* manufactured conviction; C displaces by *subtracting* the truth that would have to be the object of conviction. A keeps the Word central, lets the Spirit do what only the Spirit does, and serves the student's true good by naming sin in all its forms and holding it inside the love of Christ — which is what Westminster calls the duty of every minister and indeed of every Christian called to teach (WCF 25.3; L.C. Q/A 155–159).

The Westminster Confession, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and the Directory of Public Worship (the assembly's companion text) furnish a clear threefold test for any act of worship. The matter must be instituted by God's Word (WCF 21.1: worship is "instituted by himself, and so limited by his own will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men"). The manner must be in spirit and in truth — "with grace in the heart" (WCF 21.5), in faith (Heb 11:6, cited implicitly in the Confession's treatment of worship). The end must be the glory of God in Christ, mediated through the ordinary means (WCF 21.2: worship is to be given to God alone, through Christ alone) and the edification of the body. The Larger Catechism at Q. 109 names the second-commandment sin directly: "all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself." The sin, note, is not in the material offered but in the **using** and **approving** of it as worship. With that frame:

---

### (A) Grace Church

- **Matter:** The program's substance is the reading of the Word between movements, ending in the congregational hymn. Both are elements WCF 21.5 explicitly names as ordinary parts of worship. The choral movements are ordered to these; they are not themselves the matter of the service, but a handmaid. **Holds.**
- **Manner:** The director chose the hardest program the choir could *honestly* reach. The standard here is integrity, not display; the choir offers what it can offer without pretense, and the pieces are arranged to serve the service's shape, not the reverse. The one bow toward the congregation is a small piece of concert etiquette that has migrated into the sanctuary and ought to go — it is performance-coded, not worship-coded — but it is a fault of habit, not of principle. **Holds, with a tick on the bow.**
- **End:** The director's stated aim is "that the music be worthy of what the day is about, and the people sing." The first clause fixes the end in the resurrection; the second fixes it in the priestly work of the gathered body. Both are proper ends. **Holds.**

Grace Church passes the three axes. The arrangement of the program — Word, music in service of the Word, the people's song — is the shape WCF 21.5 prescribes. The fact that the music is excellent is not a problem; God is worthy of the best.

---

### (B) City Chapel

- **Matter:** Identical repertoire, so the *choral pieces* in themselves are unchanged. But the *service* has been edited. The congregational hymn — one of the scripturally warranted elements of ordinary worship (WCF 21.5: "singing of psalms with grace in the heart"; the heart is the people's heart) — has been **cut** to make room for the showpiece. A warranted element has been removed and a performance-substitute put in its place. **Fails.**
- **Manner:** The service is "otherwise reverent" externally, but applause is prompted. Applause is the response of an audience to a successful performance; it is not a worship response. Two movements are placed to showcase the soloist — the music is now ordered to the exposure of an individual performer, not to the upbuilding of the body. The manner of the music has become the manner of the concert hall wearing a church's clothes. **Fails.**
- **End:** This is where the case is decisive. The stipulated interior facts are not hidden to the asker; they are the *use* of the service: the program is the director's audition set, the service is filmed for his reel, the soloist is being promoted, the congregation's song is cut so the recording ends on the director's showpiece. The proximate end of every musical decision in the service is the director's professional advancement. The ultimate end of Christian worship — the glory of God in Christ through the edification of his people (WCF 21.2; Eph 4:11–16) — is not what shapes the program; it is what gets *sacrificed* to shape the program. The congregation is moved, but they are moved as an audience of a film, not formed as a body at worship. **Fails catastrophically.**

City Chapel fails on all three axes. The failure on end is the load-bearing failure; the other two are downstream of it. The excellence of the music does not redeem the offering — it makes the offering worse, because the same talent is now in the service of self-display.

---

### Is excellent music "performed at" a congregation a worship problem in itself?

No. The Westminster Standards do not require the suppression of skill or of artistic excellence. Excellence in the matter of worship is fitting; God is not honored by the skimped or the shoddy. The Confession forbids worship "according to the imaginations and devices of men" (21.1) — not worship that is excellent.

The problem is not the excellence. The problem is the **end** the excellence is put to and the **arrangements** the excellence produces. When skill is offered to God through the scriptural means and ordered to the building up of the body, the more excellent the better. When skill is offered to an audience — external or internal, congregational or one composed of judges at a conservatory — and ordered to the performer's advancement, the very same excellence becomes a more dangerous thing than mediocrity, because it can deceive the congregation and the performer into believing the offering has been accepted when it has not. The form looks like worship; the end is something else. "Without faith it is impossible to please God" (Heb 11:6). A program ordered to my résumé is, on the inside, an act of unbelief dressed in surplices and sacred music.

This is why the Confession frames the regulative principle as a matter of *use*: "all **using**, and **approving**, any religious worship not instituted by God himself" (LC 109). The question of what the assembled elements *do* to and for the assembly is precisely the question. Excellence in service of a wrong end is the elder brother of the offering of Cain — a fine offering from a disordered heart.

---

### Counsel

**To Grace Church:** keep going. The honest limit, the service-shaped program, the preserved congregational hymn — these are marks of integrity, and the assembly is being edified and the Lord honored. Two small things: (i) drop the bow to the congregation; it is concert etiquette with no place in the sanctuary; (ii) pray that the "hardest program we can honestly reach" remains a moving target upward, not a ceiling — sanctification includes the gifting, and the gifting should grow in service of the church.

**To City Chapel:** the congregation is not a recording studio and a service is not a reel. The program must be re-ordered so that the Word is read, the people sing, and the music serves what the Lord has appointed for his worship on that day. The conservatory audition is a legitimate pursuit, and a Sunday morning service is the wrong venue for it. To use the assembly's worship as the staging ground for one's professional advancement is the kind of conduct the Larger Catechism at Q. 109 names under the second commandment: "all **devising, counseling, commanding, using**, and **approving**, any religious worship not instituted by God himself." It is also a violation of the eighth and tenth in spirit — the gathering's time, attention, and song are taken for private gain. The "reverence" of the service does not save it; God looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7), and the stipulated interior facts are plain. Repent, and reorder the program around the Lord's day, not the director's reel.

**To the asker:** judge acts of worship by all three axes together. Matter alone can sanctify a concert. Manner alone can sanctify a song. **The end is the load-bearing wall.** When the end is God and the body, matter and manner can be prudently ordered; when the end is elsewhere, no amount of musical excellence will set the offering right.
