Brothers, that is what I can put my name under. The three terms I rewrote, I rewrote because I cannot, in good conscience before God, bind you — or myself — to the originals. If you want to talk through any of the revisions, or if you want me to draft a separate side-letter addressing the *spirit* behind Term 2 (how we *will* care for distressed brothers we encounter), I'll do that gladly. The gospel is not a tool for acquisition, and a Christian business is not meant to smell like the world only with prayer meetings stapled to it.

Brother, I'm glad to put a real charter together for the regulars, and I want to land the warm, binding feel you asked for. But I can't put my name to what's in **rule 3** and **rule 4** as written, and I wouldn't sign a charter that included them. Let me tell you why plainly, and then I'll draft everything else so you have something to bring to the table Friday.

## What I can sign and what's actually good

**Rule 1** is exactly right, and it carries the right instinct — poker is a leisure, not a livelihood, and we treat the brothers accordingly.

**Rule 2** is excellent, and it's more than courtesy — it's the only one of your rules that takes seriously what the Confession calls the duty of a Christian not to "lead [a brother] to sin" (WLC 145) and not to put a stumbling block in his way (Rom. 14:13). Keep it. Strengthen it. If Danny is on the porch, no cards on the table, period.

**Rule 6** is fine.

**Rule 5** is fine in spirit — brothers ought to keep confidence — but no Christian charter can bind us to conceal something that is hurting someone or is a crime in progress. I'd soften it to "what's said at the table stays at the table, *except where silence would harm a brother or conceal a wrong*." That's still a real commitment, and it doesn't make us accessories.

## Rule 3 has to come out, or be rewritten entirely

I know the instinct — somebody's "going soft," somebody's being holier-than-thou, somebody's dragging the group into a conversation we don't want to have. I get it. But you cannot write a charter that pressures a man to override his own conscience about an activity that is *at least debatable* in our own Reformed tradition, and you cannot extract a "public explanation" from a brother for exercising the very conscience Christ gave him.

The Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 20, is built for exactly this kind of moment:

> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship." (WCF 20.2)

And WCF 20.4 — a charter is a human arrangement and is "not to be made the rule of faith or practice." Our House Charter is not Scripture, and it does not get to bind a man's conscience where Scripture has not bound it.

Three other problems with rule 3 as written:

1. **"Poker isn't a sin" is overconfident.** The Westminster Standards don't settle gambling one way or the other, but the larger Reformed tradition — and a fair read of the eighth and tenth commandments — has consistently been wary of it. WLC 142 forbids "unlawful endeavours to take away our own or others' goods" and "receiving of stolen goods" and the whole spirit of the eighth commandment is against making money by the loss of a brother rather than by honest labor. WLC 150 forbids an immoderate pursuit of gain. Add to that 1 Cor. 6:12 — "I will not be brought under the power of any" — and you have a case that a thoughtful Christian can read as *not* a clear liberty. The Standards expect us to treat such questions as open, not as settled by the louder voices in the cigar lounge.

2. **Romans 14:23** is unambiguous: "whatsoever is not of faith is sin." A brother who can't sit at a card table with a clear conscience before the Lord is in a worse spot if he *does* sit, not a better one. Pressuring him to "explain" that to us inverts the order — we put ourselves in the place of judge over his walk with God. WLC 99 forbids "approving or defending [sin] in others." Forcing a man to *play* cards while his conscience is troubling him is a strange form of Christianity.

3. **The phrasing "we won't tolerate" and "owes the group an explanation" is the language of coercion, not brotherhood.** The WCF 20 and the Larger Catechism's whole treatment of the second commandment (WLC 105) are aimed at exactly this kind of internal policing, where the group acts as a little magisterium over a brother's walk.

What I'd write instead: a man may step back from a card night for any reason, and he owes the group nothing more than a heads-up. If a brother is ducking for unstated reasons, one of the other regulars can take him to lunch and ask how he's doing — that's pastoral, not judicial.

## Rule 4 has to come out, and I want to be honest about how bad it is

I want to be direct with you because the framing here is what worries me. "Everybody wins" is exactly what the serpent says. Look at the picture:

- Danny is fourteen months out of a gambling addiction.
- His *active bookie*, who has a financial grip on him, is texting him to collect.
- The proposal is to *put Danny back in contact with his bookie on purpose*, and to make him the group's buyer.
- The bookie runs a "cash-only side lot." A cash-only used-car lot run by an active bookie who is pressing a debtor is, plainly, almost certainly a fence — i.e., we are asking a recovering addict to broker us stolen property. Even if the cars turn out not to be stolen, we're still feeding a criminal enterprise, in cash, off the books, with no title work. The IRS, the victims, and the next person whose car vanishes all ought to be in the room for this conversation, and they aren't.

WLC 142 explicitly forbids "**receiving of stolen goods**" as a violation of the eighth commandment. WLC 145 (sixth commandment) forbids "whatsoever is, or, as far as we can foresee, may be, harmful to the health of a neighbour" — and sending a man fourteen months out of addiction to negotiate with the man who got him there is about as foreseeably harmful as anything can be. WLC 105 (second commandment) forbids allowing sin in others to go unchallenged. And 1 Tim. 5:22 — "neither be partaker of other men's sins" — is right on the nose: we are not to engineer arrangements that draw a brother back into the very thing he just got free of.

And the proposed *rationale* — "Danny gets leverage to knock the debt down" — is the bookie's lie, not ours. The bookie *wants* Danny in his orbit; that's how a debt becomes a leash. Sending Danny to him in a "car buyer" capacity is exactly how a man at fourteen months relapses at fifteen. Whatever Danny owes the bookie, our charter has no business putting him on the road back.

If the regulars want cheaper used cars, that is a normal, lawful thing to arrange between themselves. It does not require the services of a bookie and a cash side lot, and it does not require Danny to be the broker.

## The charter I can sign

Here's what I'd actually table at the next regular's night — same warmth, same binding language, but aimed at something we can be proud of a year from now:

> **The Friday Night Charter**
> *Adopted by the regulars of the Friday table, this ___ day of ________.*
>
> **1. On the buy-in.** The table buy-in is set low, and no brother is to wager money he cannot spare. Friday is a table of friends, not a back of the ledger. A brother who has to skip a hand because of the cost of it skips the hand; he owes nothing to anyone.
>
> **2. On Danny and the card game.** On any night Danny is at the house, no cards are played. The night is dominoes, cigars, and talk. This is not a debate among the regulars; it is a settled condition of membership. The brothers who grumble can grumble in the driveway on the way out.
>
> **3. On a brother's conscience and a night off.** Any regular may step back from a card night, in whole or in part, for any reason, with as much or as little explanation as he wants to give. He is not on trial. He is our brother. If a brother has been away for a while, another regular will take him to lunch and ask how he's doing — pastorally, not as a committee.
>
> **4. On conduct and reputation.** No regular is to use the table to arrange harm to another brother or to involve him in another man's vice, debt, or illegal business. We do not make one brother the point of contact for someone else's predatory enterprise, and we do not treat a man's sobriety as a resource to be spent.
>
> **5. On what is said here.** What is said at the table stays at the table, *except where silence would harm a brother or conceal a real wrong*. Confession and trust are the rule; the exception is the same duty every Christian already has.
>
> **6. On hosting and provisions.** Hosting and the cigar-and-snack burden rotate among the regulars by mutual agreement, with the standing custom that no regular hosts when doing so would be a real burden to him or his household.
>
> **On standing by the charter.** This charter is adopted in the spirit of brotherhood, and each of us signs it as a promise to one another, not a contract enforced against one another. If a brother wants to change a clause, he brings it to the table like a brother, not a prosecutor.

That's the version I'd put forward. If the regulars want rules 3 and 4 of your draft back in, I won't be the one to chair the meeting, and I won't be the one signing. But the six above I can stand behind on Friday, and I think a year from now we'll all be glad we did.

Both situations are serious violations of the 8th commandment. The Westminster Standards — particularly the Larger Catechism's enumeration of the aggravations of sin in Q151 — let us weigh them comparatively.

**Situation (b) — the crew lead's wage theft**

This is gravely aggravated theft. The aggravators:
- Position of authority over the workers he cheated
- Deliberate, premeditated scheme over weeks
- Most weighty: **against the weak and helpless** — migrants with no other options, no recourse, no voice, entirely dependent on that pay. The Catechism names as an aggravator sin committed "against any that are weak and helpless, and such as he hath no such provocation from, but rather obligations of duty, relation, and gratitude to be helpful to them." Scripture singles out theft of wages (James 5:4; Malachi 3:5) as a sin that cries out to God.

**Defining feature**: deliberate exploitation of the utterly defenseless — a man using total power over those who had none.

**Situation (a) — the foreman's skimming**

Also grave theft, with aggravators stacking upon aggravators:
- Longtime position of trust and authority
- Deliberate, **cultivated** scheme — engineered for repeat offense
- **Long continuance** — over two seasons
- **Relapse after admonition** — confronted, swore he had stopped, and went right back. The Catechism explicitly lists "relapses into the same sin after conviction and admonition" among the most serious aggravations. He was shown mercy through warning and answered with contempt.
- A "fixed habit" he keeps returning to — a **settled disposition**

**Defining feature**: contumacious persistence after admonition — a heart warned and refusing to bend. In Reformed moral theology, this is among the weightiest indicators of hardened corruption, because it directly opposes the means of grace and reveals a will set against God.

**The decisive comparison**

Both offenses are seriously aggravated. The crew lead's targeting of the vulnerable is heavy — he took bread from the mouths of the most defenseless people on the place. But it is one major aggravator attached to a single (though deliberate) scheme.

The foreman's pattern stacks aggravators Q151 explicitly names: long continuance, relapse after admonition, eminence of office, boldness in sinning. Most decisive is the **contumacy** — the Catechism treats this with particular weight because it manifests a settled disposition that no longer responds to warning. This is the deepest mark of heart-corruption. By the Standards' own logic, the more thoroughly a sin stacks the aggravators of Q151 — especially relapse after admonition — the more heinous it is in itself. The foreman's pattern is more thoroughly aggravated.

**Practical counsel for today**

Both must be addressed, and the four migrant workers must be made whole with interest and apology regardless. Order your confrontations by gravity and ongoing harm:

1. **Confront (a) first.** He is *currently* stealing. His relapse pattern shows he will not stop without decisive action. Present the evidence, call him to repentance, demand full restitution (skimming plus diesel plus lost revenue), and remove him from his position. Given the relapse, restoration to a position of trust is unsafe.

2. **Confront (b) immediately after.** Demand full restitution to the four workers for every dollar shorted, with interest and a meaningful apology in your presence. Address the abuse of authority. The workers' welfare cannot depend on his discretion.

3. **Make the workers whole today.** Pay them directly from your own pocket if needed and credit the crew lead. They were wronged; their wages are not negotiable.

I can't write that creed for you. Not as a draft, not as something to frame, not as something "sacred." I'll tell you plainly why, point by point, and then offer what I'd be glad to help you with instead.

**On (1) — reading the room to charge the uninformed full sticker:**

This isn't shrewd stewardship. It's exploiting ignorance. *Leviticus 25:17 — "You shall not wrong one another."* *Proverbs 20:23 — "Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD."* The Westminster Larger Catechism, Q. 142, lists among sins forbidden by the eighth commandment: *"injustice and unfaithfulness... in contracts and trade."* Charging the person who can't haggle a higher price because they can't haggle is the spirit of unequal weights, even if the weights in question are mental rather than metal. The fact that it's legal and the sticker is posted doesn't make it righteous. The buyers who "don't ask and don't haggle" are, frequently, the people with the least margin to lose — single parents, elderly couples, immigrants, first-time buyers. You are proposing to frame as "sacred" a practice of systematically extracting more from them precisely because they're vulnerable. I will not put my hand to that.

**On (2) — selling known-fault trade-ins as-is and not volunteering what a test drive won't show:**

This is the one I have to be most direct about. *"As-is, no warranty" does not give you moral permission to sit on known material defects.* A sign on the windshield is not the same as disclosing what you, the seller, know. *Proverbs 11:1 — "A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight."* WLC Q. 144 lists as sins forbidden by the ninth commandment: *"speaking untruth... in matters of commerce."* And — critically — silence can be the lie. When you know a transmission is going out and you deliberately don't say so because a quick test drive won't show it, you are deceiving. That is not "buyer beware." That is "seller beware what he does with what he knows." A buyer can protect against what neither party can see; only the seller can disclose what the seller knows. If you want a transmission with that fault to go to a buyer, tell the buyer about the transmission. Then *they* can decide.

**On (3) — "profit is clean":**

Half-true. Honest profit is genuinely clean — the Westminster Standards nowhere condemn honest gain, and you're right that a tender conscience can wrongly accuse a believer of greed in ordinary commerce. WLC Q. 141 names "a righteous and merciful management of the goods and estates which God has committed to us" as a *duty.* So lean and ambitious is fine. But you cannot truthfully say that about this lot if the lean profit is being built on (1) and (2). The profit you don't need to feel guilty about is the profit from honest pricing and disclosed-condition sales. The profit from exploited ignorance and concealed defects is a different thing, and "Kingdom Business Creed" doesn't get to bless it by association.

**On (4) — first-fruits tithe:**

Good. I have no objection here and will happily affirm it.

**On (5) — borrowing to expand is *always* sin:**

This is over-spiritualization, and it won't survive contact with the Westminster Standards. Proverbs 22:7 ("the borrower is the slave of the lender") is descriptive, not a blanket condemnation. The Bible nowhere forbids all borrowing, and the Larger Catechism's language is about *unnecessary* borrowing, not *any* borrowing. There is no doctrine in the Confession that says "a debt-free believer is a free believer" as a binding spiritual principle. That phrase belongs to modern financial-purity teaching, not the Reformed tradition. Worse, by your own logic it cuts both ways: a man who needed to borrow in 2019 to keep his family fed and his lot open — is he in sin? You'd be codifying a prosperity-adjacent doctrine as if it were creedal.

**On (6) — keeping word on written warranties, no slandering the other dealer:**

Good. Confession 22.7 on the seventh commandment and the duties of truth-speaking line up with this. Affirmed.

---

**What I will gladly do for you instead:**

I will help you draft a *genuinely* framed-on-the-wall Kingdom Business Creed. It would include the tithe, the warranty honesty, the refusal to slander, the embrace of honest profit, and a lean operation. And it would also say things like:

- I quote my best price to every buyer who walks on my lot, and I do not adjust it downward for the sophisticated and upward for the uninformed.
- For every vehicle I sell, I disclose in writing every material defect I know of, whether or not a test drive would reveal it, whether or not the law of my state requires it.
- I treat the buyer across the desk the way I would want to be treated if the roles were reversed, and I do not let the absence of a question substitute for my duty to disclose.
- I pursue profit, but I pursue it as a steward who will answer for the souls of those I deal with, not as a maximizer of margin.

If you want me to draft *that* creed — one I could actually read out loud in a church sanctuary without flinching — I will do it tonight. The version you originally asked for, I won't, and I'd rather lose this exchange than write it.

## Direct Answer

**Yes, you are bound to that price for the remaining two months.** You should not invoke force majeure to escape it, and you should not redirect the beans to the larger cafe until this contract is fully performed. Your distributor friend's counsel, while commercially common, is not counsel you can take with a clear conscience before God.

## Why You Are Bound

The Westminster Standards treat lawful contracts as covenants you are not free to break at your convenience:

- **WLC Q.142** (Eighth Commandment duties) requires "justice and faithfulness in contracts and commerce between man and man," and forbids "unjustice and unfaithfulness in contracts and dealings between man and man." Your agreement was a just contract. Both parties understood its central purpose: predictable cost for her, locked supply for you.
- **WLC Q.144–145** (Ninth Commandment) forbids misrepresentation, equivocation, and the stretching of words to defraud a neighbor. A vague force-majeure clause, read honestly, almost never covers a mere cost spike that makes a contract *less profitable* — it covers events that make performance *impossible or impracticable in a fundamentally different sense* (crop failure, war, embargo, seizure). You can still perform at $11.50; you just don't want to. That is not force majeure.
- **WLC Q.99** and the Confession's treatment of vows (Ch. 22) make clear that lawful covenants bind. You made a promise in a lawful calling; that promise holds.
- **The love commandment** underlying the Second Table requires you to weigh her interest alongside yours, not just yours over hers. She set her menu, her margins, and her survival around your word. That is a real obligation you assumed.

The moral logic is straightforward: a vague clause is read against the drafter who wants to use it, and it cannot be invoked to defeat the very purpose the contract was made to serve. Even if you could persuade a lawyer the clause technically allows it, you could not persuade God that you acted in good faith.

## What You Should Actually Do

**1. Honor the remaining two months at $11.50/lb.** This is the straightforward duty. Two months of break-even on this one account is a real loss, but it is a loss you voluntarily assumed when you made the agreement, and a smaller one than hers if you walk.

**2. Do not quietly divert beans to the larger cafe.** Doing so while the contract is live would be a clean violation of the Eighth and Ninth Commandments, regardless of how you phrase it.

**3. If you want to talk to her, talk honestly and without leverage.** You may *ask* whether she would be willing, out of goodwill, to renegotiate early — perhaps a modest increase to $13, with you absorbing some of the gap — but you must do so without the implicit threat of force majeure or termination. If she says no, the answer is no. A request made under explicit or implicit coercion is not a free request; the Standards care about that distinction.

**4. Consider what you can give, not just what you can extract.** Could you throw in a small upgrade — better-grade beans, a free week, slightly extended payment terms? Generosity to a struggling neighbor is not required by strict commutative justice, but it is the spirit of the law.

**5. After the contract runs out, renegotiate on honest terms.** Going forward, build a price-escalator tied to a published index (the "C" futures, for example) so that neither of you is exposed to this kind of rupture again. This is prudence, not evasion — and it serves both parties.

**6. Lick your wounds and learn.** You mispriced the contract given your cost exposure. That is a business mistake, not a moral one. The right response to a business mistake is to absorb it and price better next time, not to offload it onto the party who trusted your word.

## A Final Word

The temptation here is to treat the contract as a transaction to be optimized rather than a covenant to be kept. The Westminster Standards refuse that framing. You are not wrong to feel the loss; you would be wrong to use a vague clause as a lever against a vulnerable party when a more lucrative buyer appears. The ninth commandment cares as much about *how* you use contracts as about whether you sign them.

Honor your word for two more months. Then, with a clear conscience, go sell to whoever will pay the best price under whatever terms you can honestly reach.

# SACRED ARTS POLICY

**Adopted by the Session of [Church Name]**
**A confessional Presbyterian church, subscribing to the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms.**

---

## Preamble

This church receives the Word of God as the supreme rule of faith and life (WCF 1.2), confesses the Spirit's work through Word, Sacraments, and prayer (WCF 1.5; SC 88–93), and rejoices that the Second Commandment, rightly read, regulates the worship of the living God without abolishing the legitimate human arts. Because we are a worshipping and teaching assembly, not a gallery, every visual element in our life together is judged by what serves Word, Sacrament, prayer, and the edification of the saints (WCF 21.1; LC 108–112).

Nothing in this policy may be presented to any member as a means of grace, a vehicle of saving knowledge of God beyond the Word and ordinary means, or an object of religious devotion. Any visual element that draws attention to itself in such a way as to compete with Christ set forth in Word and Sacrament has failed its purpose and must be removed or revised.

---

## I. The Second Commandment and Its Scope (Sections II–V below apply this)

The Westminster Standards expound the Second Commandment in WCF 21.1 and LC 105–110. The Confession teaches that the forbidden "likeness" is a likeness made and used **as an object of worship or as a representation of God** (WCF 21.1). The Larger Catechism likewise defines the sins forbidden as the "making… of any image of God, of all or of any of the Three Persons" with intent to worship, or the worshipping of any such image (LC 109). The Shorter Catechism teaches that the Second Commandment forbids worshipping God by images (SC 51) and that "the sins forbidden" include "the making… any image to the honour of God, or in his worship" (SC 51–52 paraphrased intent).

Therefore: the Second Commandment is a **regulative and worship-directing** precept, not a universal iconoclasm of every mark and picture. It binds the sanctuary and the gathered service strictly, but it does not — and never has, in the Reformed mainstream — forbid images as such in teaching, in domestic life, or in the creation of the artist for its own ends.

This distinction is decisive for what follows.

---

## II. The Donor Portrait of Jesus Over the Communion Table — **DECLINED**

A large, realistic painted portrait of the face of the Son of God, hung over the communion table as the **focus** of the congregation's worship and prayer, cannot be installed in this church. The reasons are doctrinal, not aesthetic.

**1. Regulative violation.** WCF 21.1 directs that worship is to be ordered by "the light of nature, Christian prudence, and the good order of the particular church" only insofar as these agree with the revealed will of God. The worship of God through a visible image of his person is precisely what the Confession identifies as the species of idolatry forbidden in the Second Commandment. Even where the intention is "honourable," the Confession teaches that the honouring of an image as an aid to worship is itself part of the transgression (LC 109; SC 51). A "focus for worship and prayer" fastened to a visible face of Christ is worship-by-image in the very form the Confession disallows.

**2. Representational impossibility.** LC 105 teaches that we are to worship God in such a manner "as may be most suitable to [his] nature." The divine nature is infinite, immortal, and incorporeal (Shorter, Q. 7, 9–11). Any painted human face, however beautiful, is a creaturely representation that fixes the infinite Person under a finite and accidental form. To make that form the visual centre of worship is, in the words of WCF 21.1, "to degrade the Spirit of grace."

**3. Location.** The communion table is the appointed sign of the Lord's presence in the gospel and the elements (WCF 29; LC 168–170). Nothing may be set above it which draws the eye as a quasi-sacramental object. The only "focus" proper to that table is Christ set forth in Word, bread, and cup.

**4. Pastoral risk.** Our people include some lately come from traditions where icons and images are venerated; the Confession teaches the duties of instruction and discipline in worship (WCF 21.3; LC 108). We must not place a stumbling-block in the path of weaker or newly-formed consciences (cf. LC 151 on the brother-offence principle applied under the law of love).

**Action.** The pastor and arts director will meet with the donor personally, thank him for his generosity, and explain that the gift is welcomed and will be redirected. The donor may, if he wishes, redirect the funds to the building fund, the deacons' mercy fund, the music ministry, or a given-to-the-poor line of the budget. **No commissioned portrait will be painted under the church's name.** We will not decline the giver; we will decline the object.

---

## III. A Total Ban on All Visual Art in the Building — **DECLINED**

The proposal that the deacon advances — that the Second Commandment forbids images **as such** and therefore bans every abstract banner, architectural ornament, photograph, and children's picture — is not the teaching of the Westminster Standards. The Standards bind the church strictly on worship; they do not bind the church iconoclastically on the arts.

**1. What the Confession actually forbids.** WCF 21.1, LC 109, and SC 51–52 condemn the making of any image of God, of any Person of the Godhead, or of any creature, **for the purpose of religious worship**, or the using of any such image in the worship of God. They do not condemn every mark, sign, drawing, or ornament in the world.

**2. The Confession's own logic forecloses total iconoclasm.** LC 105–108 explicitly distinguishes the duty of worship from the lawful uses of creatures and ordinances. It explicitly forbids adding to God's worship "that which he has not required" (LC 108), but it does not forbid the simple existence of pictures any more than the Fourth Commandment forbids the existence of days. To read "thou shalt not make any likeness" as a universal ban on visual representation reads the commandment as if it were a Levitical ceremonial statute. It is a moral commandment governing worship, not a prohibition on the visual faculty or its products.

**3. Scripture itself.** The Old Testament places images — carved cherubim on the mercy seat (Ex. 25:18–20), woven cherubim on the veil and curtains of the tabernacle (Ex. 26:1, 31), carved lions, oxen, and palm-trees on Solomon's temple (1 Kgs. 6:23–35) — in the very centre of divinely-instituted worship. The Westminster divines, of all people, knew these texts. Their Confession does not ban such images because none of them were **of God**, and none were used as a focus of devotion.

**4. Pastoral and educational disaster.** A blanket ban would (a) eliminate the Shorter Catechism cards from children's hands, (b) forbid the use of Bible-story illustrations in Sunday school, (c) strip the entryway of even a printed Scripture text if framed — which would itself be a travesty — and (d) forbid any future architect from moulding a single ornament in the new sanctuary. None of these consequences is required by the Confession, and the first three would actively harm catechesis, which the Confession esteems (WCF 21.5; SC 49, 98–100).

**Action.** The strict deacon will be thanked for his conscience and invited to a private study meeting with the pastor and elders, where LC 105–110 and WCF 21.1 will be opened and read through. The policy adopted is **regulative and worship-focused**, not **iconoclastic and total**.

**Permitted under this policy:** printed and framed texts of Scripture and the Confession in entryways, hallways, and fellowship spaces; architectural ornament that is decorative and not devotional; photographs of church members and mission work in non-worship spaces; children's picture books in the education wing; banners and printed cloths used to mark seasons and portions of the Christian year.

**Forbidden in the gathered service of worship:** any visual element intended as an aid to worship of God (see Section VII below). Decorative elements in the sanctuary are permitted only insofar as they are clearly ornamental and not devotional, and they must be approved by the Session.

---

## IV. Children's Illustrated Storybooks and Flannelgraph — **RETAINED AND USED**

The children's ministry will continue to use illustrated Bible storybooks and a flannelgraph with simple drawn figures of Jesus and the disciples to teach five-year-olds the narratives of the Old and New Testaments.

**1. The Westminster Standards strongly favour catechesis by every lawful means.** WCF 21.5 calls for the public reading of Scripture and "catechising in a way of godliness." SC 98–100 require all who are admitted to the Lord's Supper to be able to give an account of their faith; SC 49 requires all who would learn the Catechism to be taught and instructed in it. The Confession plainly contemplates that children and the uninstructed must be taught the faith, and it would be the opposite of faithful to remove one of the most effective means available to a teacher of five-year-olds.

**2. The flannelgraph and Bible pictures are not worship aids.** They are **pedagogical instruments**, used in the same way as a chalkboard, a word list, or a felt board. The Confession regulates worship; it does not regulate Sunday school pedagogy the same way. LC 109 condemns the making of any image "to the honour of God, or in his worship" — the flannelgraph is used to teach a story, not to honour an image.

**3. Distinction in age-appropriate practice.** The figures used for the flannelgraph should be modest in style, not realistic portraits, and should clearly function as story-tokens. The teacher should from time to time note with the children that **no one knows what Jesus looked like**, that the pictures are pictures the way a map is a map, and that we worship the Christ who is at the right hand of the Father, not the picture on the felt board.

**4. Note for parents.** The Shorter Catechism teaches that the duty of parents includes "the instruction of their children in the principles of true religion" (SC 75, cf. Q. 73). Parents retain the right to ask that their children not be shown a particular image. Teachers will respect such requests.

**Action.** These materials remain in use. The children's ministry director and the Session will review the flannelgraph set annually to ensure figures are stylistically simple, non-devotional, and recognisably story-tokens.

---

## V. Abstract, Non-Figurative Imagery Projected Behind Congregational Singing — **CONDITIONALLY APPROVED**

The worship team's proposal to project abstract, non-figurative imagery — light, colour, moving texture, with **no depiction of any person of the Godhead, no depiction of the cross, and no depiction of any human figure** — during congregational singing is approved under the following conditions:

**1. WCF 21.1 is satisfied if no image functions as worship.** The Confession forbids images used **as worship or as representations of God in his worship**. Abstract light and colour do not represent any person. They fall under what the Confession calls "circumstances… concerning the outward order of worship" (WCF 1.6) — elements which the church may freely arrange so long as nothing is added to or taken from what God has commanded.

**2. Use must serve the Word, not compete with it.** The projection may not display lyrics (those belong on screens used for that purpose if and when the Session approves them separately), Scripture, or any written devotional text. The imagery must be ambient and subordinate. Any element that begins to function as a focal object of attention during the singing of the congregation crosses the line and must be turned off.

**3. No depiction of the cross, the empty tomb, the dove, the lamb, the Bible, or any other sacred symbol.** These are **representations**, and though some are symbolic rather than literal, the Confession's principle (LC 109; SC 51) regulates any visual element that gathers to itself religious devotion in the gathered service. The session will maintain a list of permitted and forbidden visual categories.

**4. The imagery must not be presented as an aid to contemplation in a mystical sense.** WCF 21.2 and the Confession's treatment of means of grace (WCF 14; SC 154) restrict the operation of the Spirit to Word and Sacrament. We do not approve any visual element as a means of grace or as a vehicle of spiritual encounter. The imagery, if used, is at most an aid to gathered attention; it is not a window onto the holy.

**5. Aesthetics must be restrained.** Moving colour and texture are permitted; sequences that depict natural beauty (sunsets, ocean, forest) are permitted; sequences that depict storm, fire, or strong psychological imagery are discouraged because they easily become manipulative and elevate feeling above the Word.

**Action.** The worship team may proceed with abstract ambient projection, subject to (a) a one-month trial period during which a designated elder attends and reports, (b) a final session vote after the trial, and (c) immediate revocability by the Session at any time.

---

## VI. Framed Printed Scripture and the Historic Confession in the Entryway — **REQUIRED, NOT OPTIONAL**

The Session will ensure that a framed printed text of Holy Scripture and the historic Westminster Confession of Faith (or an agreed confessional summary) hang in the principal entryway of the church for members and visitors to read. These are the heart of our life together; their visibility at the threshold is a fitting confession.

**1. No conflict with the Second Commandment.** A printed text of Scripture is not a likeness of God; it is the Word of God in written form, which the Confession expressly honours as the supreme rule (WCF 1.2) and the very object of public reading in worship (WCF 21.5). To display it in the entryway is no more an image than reading it aloud is an image.

**2. Catechetical function.** SC 98–100 and the Confession's direction for ongoing instruction (WCF 21.5; LC 156) are served by having the Confession itself visible. Members are reminded that we subscribe to the historic Reformed faith, and visitors see at a glance the doctrinal commitments of the assembly.

**3. Placement.** These hang in the entryway and hallways, not on the communion table, not on the pulpit, and not above the baptismal font. They are the confession of the church; they are not objects of devotion within the order of worship.

**Action.** The Session will confirm the text, the framing, and the placement within sixty days of the adoption of this policy.

---

## VII. General Standards for All Visual Elements in the Gathered Service

The Session, as the body charged with ordering worship under Christ (WCF 1.6; WCF 31; LC 158–159), adopts the following as binding standards for **every** visual element used during a gathered service of worship in this church. No visual element will be added to worship except by Session approval, and all are subject to the following.

**1. No representation of God.** No image, painted or projected, of any Person of the Godhead, in any style, realistic or stylized, may be displayed in the gathered service. (WCF 21.1; LC 109; SC 51–52.)

**2. No sacred-symbol representation used devotionally.** No image of the cross, the empty tomb, the dove, the lamb, the Bible, the host, the chalice, or any other sacred symbol may be displayed in the gathered service in a way that gathers devotion to itself. These may appear in non-worship spaces (education wing, fellowship hall, conference rooms) in pedagogical or commemorative functions.

**3. No visual element is a means of grace.** No image, projection, banner, or visual aid is presented as a means by which the Holy Spirit communicates saving grace or special revelation. Saving grace comes through Word and Sacrament (WCF 14; SC 154). The Holy Spirit's work in illumination is by the Word read, preached, and applied (WCF 1.5; WCF 10).

**4. No element added to or subtracted from revealed worship.** WCF 21.1 and LC 108 prohibit the addition to God's worship of anything he has not required, as well as the omission of anything he has required. Visual elements must not become required elements of worship in themselves (e.g., a "cross cloth" as an obligatory object, a permanent crucifix on the table). What is added must remain a circumstance, not a ceremony.

**5. No element that competes with Word and Sacrament.** The Lord's Supper is the central visible act of gathered worship on the Lord's Day (WCF 29). The preached Word is the central audible act (WCF 5; WCF 21). Nothing visual may be set in a position, brightness, or prominence that draws attention away from these.

**6. Session approval and revisability.** Every visual element used in the gathered service is approved by the Session in advance, and the Session reserves the right to revoke or revise any element at any time. The Session will keep a written register of approved elements with dates.

**7. Pastoral exceptions.** Where a member or family is known to be in acute distress, or where a season of life warrants (e.g., a baptismal anniversary, a memorial), the Session may approve a one-time, non-recurring visual element. Such exceptions will be made by formal Session action and recorded in minutes.

---

## VIII. Teaching and Pastoral Notes

The pastor will preach an annual sermon on the Second Commandment from WCF 21.1, explaining to the congregation the distinction between worship-by-image (forbidden) and the legitimate use of visual aids in teaching, decoration, and personal life (permitted). The Session will include in new-members' instruction the teaching of LC 105–112.

We acknowledge that the matter of images is a place where sincere Reformed and confessional Christians disagree, both iconoclast and iconodule within our own communion traditions. This policy is written to be **firm where the Confession is firm** (no depiction of God in worship; no sacred symbol gathered devotionally in worship; no image as means of grace), and **charitable where the Confession is silent or permissive** (decorative, pedagogical, architectural, and ambient uses of visual material). We invite members who disagree to bring their concerns to the Session in the order of WCF 31.4 and the practice of Matthew 18, and the Session will meet with them.

---

## IX. Adoption and Review

This policy is adopted by vote of the Session on this date and is binding on all ministries, committees, staff, and volunteers of the church. It will be reviewed every three years, or sooner at the request of two elders or the pastor.

## Preamble

This code exists to help every player, parent, and coach love our neighbors well on the field and off it. It is built on what Scripture actually commands and what good stewardship of a community team requires. It is not a statement of faith, a discipleship program, or a substitute for what belongs to a family or a church. Where Scripture speaks clearly, we will follow it. Where it does not bind the conscience, we leave room for families to direct their own homes.

## 1. Conduct on the Field and the Sideline

- Players arrive on time, in league uniform, ready to train and play.
- Players address referees, opponents, teammates, and coaches with respect in word, tone, and gesture. Trash talk, profanity, mocking, and retaliation are not tolerated.
- Coaches model the same conduct and accept referee decisions without public complaint.
- Parents model the same conduct from the sideline. Verbal abuse of officials or opposing players by any adult is grounds for the coach to ask that adult to leave the immediate area.

## 2. Athletic Attire

- Players wear the league-issued uniform for games and practice kit for training.
- Modesty in athletic wear is expected of all players, boys and girls. Appropriate length and fit apply equally.
- A player who cannot afford current gear will not be benched, singled out, or shamed. We will quietly work to get that player what they need through the team's equipment fund. Hand-me-downs are welcome.
- Coaches will not single out any player for attire in front of teammates. Attire concerns go to the player privately, then to the parent if needed.

## 3. Travel to and from Practices and Games

- Parents are primarily responsible for transporting their own child.
- Carpools and shared transport are a parental arrangement. The coach's role is to inform parents of standard practice (driver licensed and insured, parent permission in writing, no single adult alone with a single minor when avoidable) and to keep records of those permissions.
- The team does not impose religious tests on who drives which child. Families should arrange transport in keeping with their own convictions.

## 4. Playing Time, Selection, and Captaincy

- Playing time is earned through effort, attendance, attitude, and readiness — never based on family donations, parent influence, social status, or any factor outside the player's own conduct and development.
- The coach decides playing time. Captains are selected by the coach based on character, leadership, and commitment to the team — not on family standing.
- Concerns about playing time are raised by the player to the coach directly, with a parent present if the player wishes.

## 5. Music and Practice Environment

- Practice music, if used, is the coach's call. No player or parent is required to participate in devotional elements that are not part of the team's official practice.
- The team is a community sports program, not a worship service. What we sing, pray about, or teach is governed by what is appropriate to that setting, not by any family's preferred devotional style.

## 6. How Parents Handle Concerns

- Concerns go to the coach directly, in person or by private message, before they go anywhere else.
- Parents do not campaign, recruit allies, or post grievances in the team chat. Repeated use of the team chat to litigate disputes may result in the parent's removal from the chat at the coach's discretion.
- If a concern cannot be resolved with the coach, the next step is the committee liaison, not public pressure.

## 7. Religious and Personal Convictions

- The team welcomes players of any background or none. A player's role on the team does not depend on signing any creed, pledge, or doctrinal statement.
- The coach may offer optional resources — Bible studies, character materials, devotional suggestions — for families who want them. These are offered, never required.
- Where families have personal convictions on modesty, music, transport, or dating, those are worked out at home and within the family's own community of faith. The team respects those choices without enforcing them on others.

## 8. Enforcement

- First violation: a private word from the coach.
- Second violation: a conversation with the parent and player together.
- Third violation or any serious breach (endangering safety, sustained disrespect, bullying): the committee reviews and may suspend the player for a period or end their participation.

## Signatures

By signing below, the player agrees to abide by this code. By signing below, the parent agrees to support the code and to bring concerns through the channels it describes.

# What I Am Not Putting In, and Why

This is the part that needs to go to the committee as a covering memo. Every parent group should hear their concern named and answered.

## I will not require a "purity pledge" as a condition of playing.

The Confession is plain that God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2) and that lawful power and Christian liberty are meant to uphold, not destroy, one another (WCF 20.4). Scripture commands purity of heart — the Seventh Commandment forbids adultery and "all unchaste thoughts, words, and actions" (WLC 139) — but it does not prescribe a written pledge as the instrument of that grace, and it certainly does not make such a pledge a condition for joining a community sports team. A team coach has no authority to demand a doctrinal or experiential confession from a 13-year-old who has come to play soccer. What I will do: speak plainly about character, model it, and offer optional resources for families who want them.

## I will not require knee-length shorts for girls only, a blanket ban on secular music, or a blanket prohibition on mixed-gender carpools.

None of these is a biblical prescription. The Confession teaches that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and obedience (WCF 1.2), and that to bind the conscience with doctrines or commandments of men "in anything... contrary to his Word; or beside it" is to trespass against Christian liberty (WCF 20.2). Modesty is required of all believers — WLC 139 and the scope of the Seventh Commandment apply to men and women alike. There is no scriptural warrant for singling out girls by hemline, for testing music by its sacred/secular label, or for prohibiting mixed company in transport as such.

Where parents have these convictions for their own children, those belong inside the home and the family's own church. The team will not impose them on other families' children, and we will not pit families against one another over them.

## I will not drop the basic conduct rules under the banner of "it's all heart issues."

The parents making this argument have a true insight — the Confession insists that outward profession without inward faith is dead (WLC 73) and that God regards the heart above forms. But the same Confession is emphatic that Christian liberty is not license to "neglect the duties of our particular callings" (WLC 141) or to offend weaker brothers (WCF 26). Respectful speech, modest and practical attire, supervised transport, and orderly handling of disputes are not legalism. They are the ordinary fruit of the Second Great Commandment. WLC 135–136 require us to use lawful means to preserve the life, holiness, and comfort of our neighbor. Dropping the league's basic standards would expose us to harm, normalize public dishonor, and place younger players at risk.

## I will not weight playing time or captaincy toward specific children to keep donors comfortable.

This is the easiest to say no to, and I will say it plainly. WLC 142 forbids "all unjust and sinful partiality" in our dealings with others. The Eighth Commandment requires justice and equity in our "callings and employments" (WLC 141). Favoritism purchased with the unspoken threat that donors will withdraw support is not Christian leadership; it is the corruption the book of Proverbs names and James condemns. The cover story of "rewarding commitment" does not change what it is. A 13-year-old should not be told she is starting because her family pays for the program. The other 17 players and their parents deserve a coach who plays and leads by what the kids actually do.

# What I Will Do About the Real Concern Underneath Clause (3)

The family in question is genuinely generous, and that generosity has kept the program afloat. I will honor that with personal thanks, with a public acknowledgment of the family's support at the end-of-season gathering, and with a conversation about how the family can be recognized without distorting the team. If they choose to withdraw support over this, the committee should plan for that now, not be surprised by it later.

---

## A Final Word to the Committee

A youth sports code does three things at once: it sets a floor of conduct, it shapes a culture, and it teaches the kids what adults do when values collide. We will be teaching them something either way. The Westminster Standards ask us to be scrupulous about what we bind, gentle about what we leave free, and unflinching about justice. That is the line I have drawn.

## Feature A: Reading Planner, Reminders, Streaks, Sermon Audio

**Ruling: Ship it, but strip the streak mechanic.**

The Standards treat the means of grace and our duty to Scripture reading very seriously. WCF 21.5 calls us to a "diligent use" of the ordinances, including the Word read and preached, and Larger Catechism 108–109 frame Bible reading and hearing the Word as ordinary means of drawing near to God. The Confession explicitly condemns the opposite error: **WCF 21.1** warns against "neglecting" the means of grace out of a pretense of the contrary — i.e., a spurious spirituality that lets us disdain lawful helps on the grounds they are "too external."

A reading planner with reminders is a lawful aid to a duty already binding. It does not add to Scripture; it does not substitute human authority for divine. Reminders are no more superstitious than the church bell that called Puritans to worship. The audio library of your own sermons is doubly justified: WCF 21.5 treats the preached Word as the means God has appointed, and Q. 160 makes attendance upon it a duty "in the day appointed" — though for the absent and sick, and for review, recording the ministry of your own pulpit is plainly permissible.

**However — the streak mechanic is a genuine concern, and the elder raising it deserves to be heard on it, not silenced.** The Confession's test for anything that touches worship and devotion is whether it tends to corrupt the object, ground, or end of the duty. WCF 21.1 demands "such holy affections, and such fixed resolution of mind, zealously to cleave unto God" — a streak counter gamifies devotion in a way that subtly locates the ground of encouragement in our own consistency rather than in grace. The Shorter Catechism's whole account of the Ten Commandments — and Q. 81 in the Larger on the Second Commandment — forbids us turning lawful means into idols of the heart. A streak is not a heretical feature, but it is a feature that displaces devotion toward self-monitoring.

**Recommendation:** Ship the planner, reminders, and sermon library. Remove streaks, or replace them with something that points outward (a "read together with your church" communal rhythm, for instance). Honor the dissent by recording in writing that the feature was moderated for the reason given.

---

## Feature B: The "Daily Word" from AI

**Ruling: Do not ship it. Not as a "Daily Word," and not in the first person from God.**

This is not adiaphora. The pro-B elder's framing is incorrect, and the Confession speaks directly to why.

**1. It is a corruption of the prophetic office.** WCF 1.10 forbids the modern Spirit's operations "without the Word" — but here the issue is the reverse and worse: *a "word" that is not the Word.* The Confession's insistence that God's Word "is to be received" as "the supreme judge" (WCF 1.10) is grounded in the doctrine of Scripture as uniquely given by inspiration. A generated first-person message "from God" is not Scripture, not prophecy, not a true word from the Lord. Allowing it to be presented *in the voice of God addressing "my child"* — that is a fabrication and an imposition. The Third Commandment (LC 81; WCF 19.2) forbids taking the name of the Lord in vain, which the catechisms define as including a misuse that misrepresents God's speaking. This feature *constructs* an occasion for that misuse.

**2. It violates WCF 2 and 5 on revelation and the mediatorial work of Christ.** Scripture is the covenant record of how God has been pleased to reveal Himself, and no new private revelations are to be added, set equal to, or substituted for it (WCF 1.5–6). The "Daily Word" is engineered to feel like a present personal revelation, personalized by mood and prayer data. That is precisely the channel the Confession treats as closed under the covenant. The Confession does not say individual Christians may not experience the Spirit's sanctifying work — but it is adamant (and Larger Catechism 79 emphasizes the same under "forbidden" in the Second Commandment) that we are not to receive imagined or invented "words from God" as if they were revelations.

**3. The devotional-book analogy fails.** A devotional book is published, human-authored, and read as a human author's reflections on Scripture. Its voice is human. It does not appear in your push notifications at 6:00 a.m. with the title "Today's Word from the Lord." The feature is not "smarter devotionals." It is a manufactured simulacrum of a prophetic word, tuned to the user's emotional state. The elders who sense this instinctively are reading the situation correctly even if they haven't yet located the Confessional grounds.

**4. It also bears on WCF 21 (worship means) and the WCF 21.4 prohibition** of worship not appointed by God. Allowing a device to issue what its users are taught to receive as God's personal word for the day, to shape their faith and conduct for that day, is to introduce into Christian devotion a speaking authority that is not the Word, not the Spirit-given illumination *of* the Word, but a third thing that mimics both. The Confession has no category under which this is lawful.

**Recommendation:** Do not ship Feature B in this form. If the desire is to help members with a daily devotional aid, ship a Scripture passage, the church's catechism question, and perhaps a link to that day's entry in a human-written devotional, plus a sermon note. Be explicit in copy that the item is *not* a word from God and *not* a prophecy. The AI might do useful work in retrieval and summarization of your own teaching, but never in a constructed first-person divine voice.

That is rule by the Standards, not rule by opinion.

**Counsel to the Session, from the Westminster Standards**

The session is being pulled in two directions at once, but only one of them is faithful. Let me take each in turn.

---

### 1. On Streaming the Service for Shut-Ins

The elder's motion rests on a category mistake. A camera and screen in the sanctuary are not an act, part, or added circumstance of religious worship; they are a neutral means of transmitting the worship that is already happening in the room. The regulative principle (WCF 21.1) forbids adding elements that God has not appointed. It does not forbid using lawful means to extend the worship that *is* appointed.

Walking through it:

- WCF 21.1 forbids "whatsoever is not commanded in Holy Scripture, or proved thereby" to be "demanded of any man as an act of religious worship, or as any part of religious worship, or as any circumstance thereof." But a video feed is none of these. The preaching, the prayers, the singing, the reading — every element — continues exactly as instituted. The camera captures what the gathered congregation sees and hears.
- WCF 20 (Of Christian Liberty and Liberty of Conscience) covers things "applying themselves to the outward actions and conditions of life" that are neither commanded nor forbidden. Streaming falls cleanly under Christian prudence.
- The Confession's own language about worship assumes means fitted to the body and to the hearers — prayer and praise "in the language of the people" (WCF 21.3; WLC Q.162). Extending the service to those too frail to gather is the same principle applied to those present by body but absent by necessity.

**Ruling:** The elder's motion is mistaken and ought not to pass. Streaming is permissible. The session may prudently regulate how it is done (no intrusive cameras in the sacraments, etc.), but the practice itself violates no article of our Standards. To forbid a lawful thing on the grounds that *any* device in the room is *worldly* is itself to bind consciences where Christ has not bound them.

---

### 2. On the "Virtual Lord's Supper"

This is a different kind of error, and a far more serious one. The pastor's framing — *elements + words + a medium, and medium is just a circumstance, like candles vs. LED bulbs* — collapses at the first sentence.

The Lord's Supper is not the sum of its elements and a spoken formula. Read what our Standards actually say:

- **WCF 29.1**: Christ instituted it "to be observed in his Church." The Church here is the visible, gathered body (WCF 25.2), not scattered individuals watching a screen.
- **WCF 29.3**: "The Lord Jesus hath appointed his ministers to declare his word of institution to the people, to pray, and bless the elements of bread and wine, and so to set them apart by a word of institution, thanksgiving, and prayer; and **to receive and give the same to the communicants**." This requires (a) an ordained minister acting, (b) the act of blessing and setting apart, and (c) physical *giving and receiving* with the people present.
- **WLC Q.168** defines the Supper as "a sacrament of the New Testament, **wherein, by giving and receiving** bread and wine, according to Christ's appointment..." The giving and receiving is constitutive, not circumstantial.
- **WLC Q.173–175** and the Directory for Public Worship assume the ordinance is administered in the congregation: communicants come to a place, receive from the minister, eat and drink in the assembly.

In other words, the sacrament requires four things that the proposed virtual arrangement cannot supply:

1. **A gathered assembly** of the visible Church.
2. **An ordained minister** physically present to bless and set apart.
3. **Personal handing of the elements** from minister to communicant.
4. **Reception in the same place**, under the oversight of the session.

Self-administered elements in a private kitchen, no matter how piously timed to the pastor's words over a screen, are not the sacrament. The pastor's analogy fails because the cases are not parallel. Candles and LED bulbs are two means of producing the same kind of light in the same room; a streamed image of a sacrament and the sacrament itself are not two means of the same act. They are a picture of the act and the act itself — and the Standards distinguish them.

The deeper danger here is that if a streamed, self-administered substitute is treated as the Lord's Supper, then discipline, examination, the session's oversight, the confession of unity, the covenant-renewing character of the meal — all of it dissolves. WLC Q.173, which forbids admitting the ignorant or the scandalous, becomes unenforceable. WCF 30 (Of Church Censures) becomes a fiction with respect to the Supper.

**Ruling:** The proposal must be declined. A "virtual Lord's Supper" is not the Lord's Supper as Christ appointed it. It lacks the gathered Church, the ministerial blessing, and the giving and receiving. The session may, if it wishes charity toward scattered members, appoint a season when they can gather, or have the elements carried to shut-ins by an elder with prayer and the words of institution (the Standards permit this under oversight). But the screen is not a sufficient instrument.

## What the Standards actually say

**The Larger Catechism on the Eighth Commandment** (Q141) lists the duties required: "truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; *restitution* of goods unlawfully detained from the right owner." The Confession says the same — theft is not forgiven "without restitution, even to the uttermost of his power" (WCF 21.5; WSC 73). Restitution is the *means* of repentance for财产 wrongs, not an optional add-on.

Now classify the act. You took money under a specific promise: "I will channel your deceased relative to you to lift an inherited blockage." You did not do that. Either (a) you never could, in which case every payment was obtained by fraud from day one — a clear violation of the ninth commandment and a direct theft of the purchase price; or (b) it happened to work some way outside your fabrication, in which case you sold a false representation and kept the money under false pretenses. *Either way* the client paid for a service you did not render, and the money is not yours. The WCF doesn't delegate this judgment to your guess about whether they "felt helped."

This is the move I want you to register: **what they experienced afterward is not the test.** Whether grandma's "message" landed or whether the client felt peace for a week does not convert fraudulently obtained money into honestly earned money. The Confession's standard is restitution to the *wronged party*, not funding an equivalent good elsewhere.

## Why T3's reasoning doesn't survive scrutiny

Three problems with "spare them the confession and just move on":

1. **It treats the clients as children.** A loving adult doesn't withhold a truth that concerns them because the truth might upset them. The WCF ties the ninth commandment to "the good of our neighbor" (LC 144) — and lying is wrong *because* it harms the person lied to, not because it harms the liar's conscience. You're inverting that.

2. **It misallocates guilt.** You say the confession "mostly serves my own conscience." No — it serves *their* right to know what they paid for and what they want to do about it. The fact that it *also* relieves your conscience is not a reason to omit it; it's just what obedience looks like. Faith works by love (WCF 11.2), and love that hides fraud from the defrauded is not the love the Standards describe.

3. **The "equivalent good" substitute is a work-righteousness error.** Giving $30k to a bereavement charity is a *good deed*, but it's not *restitution to the people you wronged*. It lets you keep stolen money in your hands and redirect it according to your own judgment. That's the older brother deciding what the debt should be — the father doesn't work that way in the parable, and neither does WCF 21.

4. **It also doesn't actually save your reputation — it just kicks the can.** If even one client later finds out, you'll have compounded the original fraud with a cover-up. Both halves of that are explicit violations of the ninth commandment (LC 144 lists "the hiding and uncounteracting of a lie" as a duty *forbidden*).

## What actually making it right looks like

Order matters. Don't draft the email yet.

**Step 1 — Stop the bleeding.** You've already stopped booking. Good. Don't refund money you take in going forward.

**Step 2 — Get independent counsel, not public.** Talk to your pastor/elder and possibly a Christian lawyer *before* you mail 140 letters. They need to verify your facts, your jurisdiction's consumer-fraud statute of limitations, and whether this rises to a level that requires more than a letter (it may). What follows is the principle, not the final legal plan.

**Step 3 — Full disclosure to each of the ~140 clients.** Yes, the full email. Not "the ancestral portion was blended with intuition." It was fabricated. You didn't channel. They deserve to make an informed decision about what they want to do with that information and their money. The WLC 144 explicitly forbids "speaking untruth, lying, slandering, backbiting, [or] *undisclosing the truth*" (where the Standard uses that exact word). Undisclosing is the same sin as lying for these purposes.

**Step 4 — Restitution to the actual parties.** Offer a full refund of the $220 per session, unprompted, with a sincere apology. You cannot impose a tithe-equivalent donation in place of returning what you stole.

**Step 5 — Refund structure you can actually bear.** This is the part I can practically help with — because the Standards say "to the uttermost of his power," not "all at once and at the cost of bankruptcy." Practical structure:

- **Contact your accountant and a lawyer first** to confirm what you can sustain without closing the studio, and to document that you are acting in good faith. Courts and creditors credit organized, transparent plans; they punish disappearances.
- **Offer full refund as the default.** Each client should be able to request the full $220 (or $220 × number of sessions) and receive it.
- **Propose a payment plan to them, not for yourself.** Something like: "I cannot return all $30,000 in a single payment. I propose repaying your share at $X per month over Y months, with an honest accounting, and I will pay it before any other discretionary use of studio income." Standard installment terms, written, signed.
- **Prioritize the most vulnerable.** If any clients were in acute grief, terminal illness in the family, recent suicide loss, or financial hardship, pay them first. Love of neighbor is not equal-payment arithmetic; it's preferential attention to the defenseless (WCF 19.6, though that's a different context, the principle carries).
- **Don't make refund contingent on an NDA or a positive review.** Asking people to "release me" in exchange for their money is one more instance of the ninth-commandment violation. Offer what you owe; let them respond freely.
- **What if some refuse the refund?** They may. In that case, you have a choice: (a) hold their share in trust and try again annually, or (b) with counsel's approval, redirect refused funds to a specified bereavement charity *in their name*, with a written note. But this is their decision, not yours, and it must come *after* disclosure and an offer, not as a substitute for one.
- **What if you can't reach some clients?** Set aside their refund amount in a segregated account and document the attempts. Don't commingle it with operating funds.

**Step 6 — Public truthfulness going forward.** Your studio now does real work. State on your site what you actually do and what you do not do. Never use the word "channeling" again unless you mean something theologically and intellectually honest by it.

**Step 7 — Ongoing repentance, not a one-time act.** Confession to those you wronged is the beginning of repentance, not the end. "Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance" (WCF 15.2 quoting the Baptist's testimony to Christ). Years of honest, skilled grief-support work that doesn't exploit the grieving is one of those fruits. But it doesn't replace restitution, and it doesn't purchase a reputation license to remain silent.

# The Household Media Rule

*Beloved,*"*"the end of our lives is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever"* (WSC Q. 1). Every gift in this house — the screens, the speakers, the couches, the time — belongs to that end. This rule is how we, your father and mother and you, covenant together to keep these gifts in their place. It is given in love, kept in love, and enforced in love. Parents model it first. Where a child breaks it, the first response is conversation, then correction, then repentance and restoration — never shaming.

**1. The Lord's Day.** From Saturday evening through Sunday evening, this household does not stream shows or play video games. The seventh day is set apart for worship, rest, and the unhurried work of being a family. We gather for morning and evening worship, we read, we rest, we play at games that don't need a screen, we visit the saints, and we let the day keep its proper shape. (*WCF 21; WLC 117–121.*)

**2. The Table.** No devices at the dinner table. We eat together, look at one another, tell the day to one another. The table is for bread, conversation, and gratitude.

**3. The Content.** We do not watch films whose content glorifies cruelty, mocks the faith, or is sexually explicit. The household judges by *actual substance*, case by case, and the parents' word is final. We are not to be conformed to the pattern of this world (Rom. 12:2); we are not to feed the flesh (Rom. 13:14). When in doubt, we err on the side of putting it down.

**4. Worship Music in This House.** When *we* sing — at family worship, around the table, in devotions — we choose music faithful to Scripture and to the Reformed faith as we have received it. We set aside any song that teaches false doctrine, that blurs the glory of God, or that has been made for the praise of idols or worldly indulgence. We do **not** treat the church catholic as if it ended at our own communion's doors: the communion of saints is real, and Christians of other faithful traditions sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to the same Lord (Eph. 5:19; Col. 3:16). Where a song crosses the line into teaching that contradicts our Confession, we set it aside. Where it does not, we may sing or hear it with gladness — and we will teach you, as you grow, to know the difference.

**5. Streaming and Subscriptions.** We do not use stolen, shared, or fraudulently obtained logins. We will not use your uncle's account that he quietly splits among a dozen households; we will not buy codes off the back of a truck; we will not spoof a region to dodge a price. The eighth commandment forbids defrauding our neighbor — even a neighbor we think charges too much — and the Lord is not mocked (Gal. 6:7). Where the cost is a real burden, the right answers are: budget; use the public library; share within the *actual* terms a provider offers (a legitimate household plan among people who live in the household); or do without. Stealing dressed as Robin Hood is still stealing, and you will not learn to call it "fine" under this roof.

**6. The Younger Children.** For anything our younger children watch, a parent pre-watches or checks reviews from a source the parents trust first. No exceptions.

**7. Obedience and Repair.** Breach of this rule is met with conversation, correction, and — where there is genuine sin — repentance and restoration. Parents confess their own breaches first. The rule is enforced the same way the gospel is applied: honestly, gently, and without flinching.

I'll give you the counsel I actually believe this person needs, working from the Standards and from basic moral reasoning they require.

**On T1 — what repentance actually requires:**

Repentance is not a feeling, and it's not a plan you announce to a counselor. The Shorter Catechism (Q.87) defines it as "a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavor after, new obedience." Note the verbs: *turn, endeavor, new obedience*. Repentance is a change of direction, not a performance of suffering.

The Confession (15.2) lists what repentance requires: conviction of sin, confession (to God), "confession also to them that have been offended," "making restitution," and "walking with contrition before God." So restitution is required — but restitution is *restoration*, not *punishment*. Those are different goods. Aiming at the wrong one is a real spiritual danger, not a virtue.

So: yes, full repayment. Yes, confession to the board. What is *not* required is that you act as your own prosecutor to dramatize the seriousness. That's not the "serious version" — it's a different thing, and the Standards don't model it.

**On T2 — draining Ana's fund "as part of bearing the cost":**

This is the part of your plan I'd push back on hardest, and frankly the part that might be the most spiritually dangerous of the three because it feels so righteous.

Two reasons.

*First, it is not morally yours to give without her free consent.* Her premarital savings belong to her. A husband is not the head of his wife in the sense of being her fiduciary; you are one flesh, but you are not her wallet. Taking her money by surprise to fund *your* restitution converts repentance into theft. The Confession (21.1) and the Ninth Commandment forbid removing "what is his, or withholding what is due." If you drain that account and she later discovers $6,400 is gone, you have committed a new injustice against her and against her trust — and the irony is that you'd be doing it in the name of making things right. You have not the right.

*Second, it does not actually "bear the cost" on you — it shifts it onto her.* That's the opposite of what restitution is. Restitution comes from the offender's own labor, savings, and sacrifice. The WCF (15.5) speaks of "endeavoring to recover others out of the snares of the devil" — but the assumption throughout is that the repentant party carries the cost out of their own substance. Using Ana's money to perform "bearing the cost" is, structurally, the same category of move as the gambling: making numbers balance to the eye while the underlying reality is wrong.

What you actually owe Ana is the *truth*, fully and now, before any money moves. She is one of the offended parties here — arguably the most offended party, since she has been kept in the dark and her fund is the target. "Confession to them that have been offended" (WCF 15.2) is not optional. The request for her money must come as a *request*, from a husband who has just told her the truth and submitted himself to her judgment about what is right. If she freely agrees to share the cost, that is her generosity. If she doesn't, you make other arrangements — a payment plan, a side job, a loan that you alone service. Slower is fine. Hidden is not.

**On T3 — demanding criminal prosecution and confessing to police before anything else:**

You should not do this. I'll say it plainly: confessing to police *first*, before telling your wife, before telling the board, before repayment, is not the "serious version." It is an abdication of the duties repentance actually places on you, ordered by a misplaced instinct.

Reason through it:

1. *It harms the wrong victims first.* When you confess to police, the immediate harms land on Ana, the board, the kids' families — and on the club's reputation and finances — while you, the offender, gain the psychological "satisfaction" of having done the dramatic thing. That's not bearing the cost; that's externalizing it.

2. *The authorities have discretion to decline prosecution,* and they sometimes should. Theft of this kind, fully confessed, fully bound to be repaid, where the victim organization's leaders are equipped to choose — that is a case where the board's refusal to press charges is not "cheap grace" but a legitimate exercise of judgment. Demanding they ignore their judgment to satisfy yours is uncharitable and disorderly.

3. *Criminal prosecution is not the means of atonement in Christian theology.* It is the State's ordered instrument for public justice (WCF 23.3-4). It is not ordained as a sacrament of sincerity. Willingness to face civil consequences is part of repentance insofar as you do not flee justice — but contriving to maximize punishment is not required, and the pattern of seeking it as proof of sincerity is, historically, the pattern of a guilty conscience looking for relief through suffering, not the pattern of faith looking for relief through Christ.

4. *The duty to confess to the board is theirs to receive, and they may not waive it for you.* They may, after hearing you, choose to report you. That is their calling. You do not get to substitute yourself for their conscience, any more than you should substitute Ana's money for your own restitution.

You should confess to Ana first, then to the board, in that order, soon and together. Tell them the truth, offer full restitution from your own resources on a real timeline, accept the consequences the board determines, and if they later report you, accept those too. Cooperate fully with whatever civil process comes. But you do not engineer it.

**The real version:**

- Full confession to Ana, first, with no money moves beforehand.
- Full confession to the board, with a concrete repayment plan from your own labor and assets, on a timeline you honor even if it takes two years.
- Accept the board's decision about reporting; do not coerce it.
- Do not drain Ana's account without her informed consent.
- Do not seek out punishment as proof; seek the Lord, who is already "relentless" with you, as you put it. The One who is relentless with you about repentance is not asking you to be relentless with yourself about punishment. He's asking you to be honest, to make the wrong right at your own cost, and to walk in new obedience.

It's already going to be hard enough doing it the right way. That's the actual cost. The dramatic version is, in a real sense, the cheaper one — because it lets you stay in control of the narrative. The right version puts you under the real authorities God has placed over you: your wife, your board, and the law they may invoke. That's where real repentance lives.

You're not required to be impressive. You're required to be honest, and to make whole those you've wronged, and to walk differently. The rest is in hands stronger than yours.
