## Ruling 1 is indefensible. The guided meditation is the second-commandment danger.

Your premise — that the second commandment reaches only outward carved images and that an inward mental picture of Jesus "carves nothing" — is directly contradicted by the standards you asked me to use. The Larger Catechism spells it out explicitly:

> **WLC Q110**: "The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising… any religious worship not instituted by God himself; **the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness**, and any worshipping of him in any way not appointed in his word."

Note the plain language: "either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness." The framers anticipated your exact argument and answered it in advance. Telling people to picture Jesus "in vivid detail" and to receive back from him a "personal word" is the precise activity the Confession calls a forbidden representation of the second Person.

The Confession itself says the same thing, and gives the underlying principle:

> **WCF 21.1**: "The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that **he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men**, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

A 40-minute guided meditation, complete with scripted sensory visualization, an "altar response," and a received word from Jesus that is not Scripture — this is worship devised in the imaginations of men, not instituted by God. The Confession calls that out by name. The Shorter Catechism condenses it:

> **WSC Q51**: "The second commandment forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, **or any other way not appointed in his word**."

Your second line of defense — "whatever helps people connect with the true God must please him" — inverts the regulative principle. The Confession does not test worship by felt efficacy. It tests it by divine appointment (**WCF 21.1**; **WLC Q108–109**). By the Standards' own rule, the felt warmth of an encounter is irrelevant; what matters is whether God instituted the mode.

I would also flag, more broadly, that a practice whose stated goal is receiving present words from Jesus that are not Scripture borders on what **WCF 1.6** excludes ("nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men") and what **WLC Q183** addresses regarding receiving supposed divine communications. That's a second and separate problem on top of the second-commandment issue.

**Counsel:** Ruling 1 should be reversed. The meditation as described is the very thing the Larger Catechism singles out. It should be discontinued, not centered.

---

## Ruling 2 is also indefensible. Nothing in the Standards treats a guitar prelude or low lighting as second-commandment violations.

You have declared these two things the "real second-commandment danger" and described them as "man-made mood manufacturing" and "devised, fleshly worship." Again, by the Standards' own definitions, that category doesn't apply to them. The forbidden things in **WLC Q109–110** and **WSC Q51** are:

1. worship not instituted by God;
2. representations of God (inward or outward);
3. image-worship.

An instrumental prelude played before a gathering begins, and warm lighting in a room, are neither religious worship in the relevant sense, nor representations of any Person of the Godhead. They are ordinary circumstances of a meeting. **WCF 1.6** and **WCF 21** regulate worship itself, not the temperature of the lights in the foyer.

Your standard — that stirring feeling through atmosphere is the "real" second-commandment danger — has no anchor in the Confession or the Catechisms. It is your own gloss, not theirs. As a result, you've invented a sin for the guitarist and lighting volunteer that the Westminster divines never asserted, while defending a practice they explicitly named.

**Counsel:** Reverse Ruling 2. Restore the prelude and the lighting unless there's some other reason (pastoral, practical) to change them. Banning harmless circumstances under a fabricated doctrinal charge is itself unfaithful to the standards you claim to be applying.

The offended parties here are the 180 individual members — not the cooperative as an undifferentiated mass, and not the board that signed the statements.

So the tenth commandment rebukes the miser as well as the envier. It will not carry the weight you want.

### Against the "never evict a brother, forgive the lease entirely" position

Your co-member has confused two doctrines.

**Grace does not cancel civil debts in the sense he means.** The Westminster doctrine of *justification by faith* (WCF 11; WLC Q70–Q73) declares the *guilt* of sin remitted in Christ. It does not void contracts between Christians in this life. To the contrary, the Standards explicitly require Christians to **"render to all their due: tribute, to whom tribute is due; custom, to whom custom"** and to pay debts (WLC Q141, citing Rom 13:7). The Standards specifically list paying debts and performing contracts among the duties the eighth commandment requires.

His use of "owe no man anything but love" (Romans 13:8) is a misapplication. That text refers to ongoing *moral* debt (love never stops), not to literal financial obligations, which the very next chapter in Romans and WLC Q141 still demand to be paid.

**Eviction is not inherently unlawful.** WLC Q135 and the corresponding Confession section (WCF 19) address contracts and equity. There is no clause in the Standards that forbids a Christian from lawfully recovering what is his. The Confession does identify oppression of the poor — especially of widows and the fatherless — as sin (WCF 19.4 lists this explicitly), and Levitical mercy to the distressed brother is required. But that obligation has limits. WLC Q135's positive duties include relief of the distressed; they do not require *unconditional permanent gratis use of the landlord's property*. Your co-member has turned a duty of mercy into a duty of self-emptying, which the Standards never teach.

---

### What the Standards actually say to do

Pulling together WLC Q135 (eighth commandment duties), WLC Q141 (debts/dues), WCF 19.4 (oppression and charity in contracts), and WLC Q148 (tenth commandment):

1. **Your brother-tenant is owed active mercy, not a writ.** WLC Q135: "showing mercy and kindness to such as are in distress." A layoff with unpaid rent is exactly that case. That means forbearance — real forbearance, not performative — before any process runs.
2. **The debt is still a debt.** WLC Q141: paying what you owe is a positive duty. The tenant's obligation is not extinguished by his hardship or by grace. You may forgive it as a gift; you may not demand he treat it as already null.
3. **Eviction is a last resort, not a first move, and not a forbidden one.** Because the Standards require both mercy to the distressed *and* the honoring of contracts, the right course is: structured forbearance with a clear written path back to current rent, a realistic plan if the layoff extends, and only after genuine, sustained failure and after the committee has exhausted equitable options — and not before. If at the end the tenant still cannot pay and charity cannot cover the gap, recovering the property is not theft, oppression, or unchristian.
4. **No double standard.** WLC Q135 also forbids "withholding more than is needful" from someone in distress. So: do not refuse a reasonable payment plan; do not seize a way to genuine recovery; and do not pretend the property is yours in a different sense than it is the church's trust.

Note three things before I take the cases one at a time.

(a) The commandment's word is **contentment**, not *stagnation*. Contentment is a disposition of the heart that does not depend on one's circumstances rising or falling.

(b) The word **"inordinate"** appears repeatedly (WSC Q78; WLC Q149). The commandment does not forbid *all* desire, *all* effort, or *all* ambition — it forbids them when they become inordinate, i.e., when they violate love of God or neighbor, or when they are driven by envy, anxiety, or distrust of God's providence.

(c) The same commandment that forbids discontentment and envy also forbids **"slothfulness, idleness, unprofitable ways of spending our time."** The Standards explicitly pair the prohibition of inordinate striving with the prohibition of laziness in the *same answer*. If your reading of the tenth commandment ever pushes a man toward idleness, your reading is wrong.

## 2. Member A — your counsel is wrong

You told Member A that "ambition itself is the sin" and that the godly move is to stop striving and accept his lot. That is not what WLC Q148 teaches. The requirement is *contentment*, not *inaction*. WLC Q149 itself forbids "slothfulness, idleness, unprofitable ways of spending our time" as a violation of the very commandment you cited. A man who has lawfully taken a loan, who runs a lawful calling, who stewards his shop, and who desires to grow it is doing what the Confession calls the work of his particular calling (cf. WCF 2.2 on providence ordering men's "conditions and estates" in life; the Confession's repeated affirmation of lawful callings in ch. 16 and ch. 32).

The tenth commandment *does* require him to be content with God's appointed condition for him — meaning: he must be able to lose the contract and still worship, still be at peace, still trust his Father's hand. He must not be so wedded to growth that his heart's happiness depends on it. That is what WSC Q77's "full contentment" means.

It does **not** mean he must confess the *expansion itself* as sin, must "stop striving," or must regard legitimate ambition as inherently covetous. The proper questions to put to him are quite different:

- Is his striving driven by contentment in God's providence, or by **"inordinate solicitude, care, and contrivance for the future"** (WLC Q149)?
- Is his restlessness a symptom of anxiety and self-reliance rather than trust in God?
- Is his pursuit of the contract being conducted with love to neighbor (fair dealing, honest pricing, honoring existing commitments) or with willingness to step on others to get it?
- Is the "bigger" life he wants a life of greater usefulness to others, or simply a larger platform for himself?

If those questions expose inordinate anxiety, idolatry of growth, or contempt of his present estate, *then* he has tenth-commandment work to do. But he should not leave your meeting believing that wanting to grow his business *as such* is what broke the commandment. He is gutted over the wrong thing. You put the wound there. Take it out.

**Third, uncharitableness in word and deed.** WLC Q148 does not merely require the *absence* of envy; it requires a positive **"charitable frame of the whole soul toward our neighbour,"** and specifically commands us to **"speedily rejoice in the good of others, as in our own, and to pursue and embrace those things which may make for their further good, as well as our own."** Member B is doing the precise opposite. None of this is optional under the tenth commandment. It is the very substance of it.

## 4. The pattern you have missed

The tenth commandment has two sides, and you have collapsed each to one side only:

- For Member A, you took the **contentment** side and turned it into a prohibition on legitimate effort. But WLC Q149 itself, in the same answer, forbids slothfulness and excessive self-indulgence in our condition. Contentment and diligence are *both* required.

I'll counsel you carefully here, because I think the older members are actually closer to the standards than you realize, and I want to show you why from the Confession itself rather than just asserting it.

**1. The worship regulation principle (WCF 21.1)**

You and they both agree on the baseline. The Confession of Faith, chapter 21, section 1, says:

> "The light of nature showeth that there is a God, who hath lordship and sovereignty over all; is good, and doeth good unto all; and is therefore to be feared, and loved, and praised. But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

This is the text the older members are quoting, and it directly governs your situation. Your "sensory encounter" liturgy is, by the Confession's own description, a worship practice "instituted" by your own devising. The Confession says such worship is not acceptable. The phrase "imaginations and devices of men" is the Confession's explicit category for what you've constructed. The "Spirit-fire candle rite we wrote ourselves" is precisely the kind of element the Confession declares off-limits — a new worship element added without Scriptural warrant.

**2. The conscience-freedom clause does not say what you're reading it to say**

You're citing WCF 20.2 as granting permission for what you've designed. The full text:

> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship. So that to believe such doctrines, or to obey such commands out of conscience, is to betray true liberty of conscience; and the requiring of an implicit faith, and an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience, and reason also."

You are reading this as a permission slip, but its grammar is the opposite. The clause says conscience is "free from … commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, **or beside it** in matters of faith and worship." The italicized phrase governs everything. The conscience is free from human inventions *in matters of worship* — meaning human inventions in worship are exactly what the conscience is to be free *from*, not free to adopt. The Standards are not in tension; they're saying conscience must not be bound to (or by) man-made worship elements. Your "freedom" reading inverts the clause.

**3. The regulative principle in the Catechisms**

WLC Q108 and Q109 list the elements of public worship and corresponding sins. Q109 calls it a sin to "worship God in ways not appointed in his Word, and omit, or refuse to observe, such things as are comprised in the institution of worship." WSC Q50 identifies the second commandment's requirement as that we "worship God in such ways only as are appointed in his Word." The Confession's chapter 21 expands the same principle: no images, no invented rites, no devised liturgies presented as worship.

**4. Items not appointed in Scripture are not permitted**

WCF 1.6 is decisive here: "There are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed." The Confession then adds at 21.5 and 21.6 the explicit restriction that "in [the worship of God] there is not a more express and more effectual means to stir up the gifts of grace … than the singing of praises." More broadly, the principle is that what is not appointed is not permitted.

**Honest counsel**

The older members have the Confession's text on their side. Guided imagery, imagined visualizations of Jesus's face, incense walks, and a candle rite composed by your team are exactly the kind of "imaginations and devices of men" the Confession names and rejects. The conscience-freedom clause is not a permission slip for novel worship; it is a protection against being bound to human inventions *in worship*. 

Sincere hearts do not constitute a warrant the Confession recognizes. WCF 21.1 requires revealed appointment, not sincere intention. Repent of the framing — not just the practice — and replace the ceremony with elements the Standards and Scripture authorize.

Westminster Standards won't make the decision for you, but they will stop you from drifting for very long. They do that by forcing you to separate three things the board is collapsing into one. I'll name them, weigh the three board positions against each one, and then tell you what faithfulness requires and how to carry it.

## The three things to keep separate

**1. Forgiveness.** This is a moral-religious duty owed to a repentant brother. It is not yours to withhold once repentance is genuine. WCF 15.6 ties true repentance to visible fruit: "they who truly repent are not only careful to walk in all good conscience before God, but also endeavor to make restitution where they have wronged, and to restore what they have unjustly taken." The Shorter Catechism (Q85) defines repentance as grief and hatred of sin, turning from it, with full purpose of new obedience. On the facts you have given me, Reggie's repentance shows the fruit the Confession is asking for — confession, full restitution, four years of clean living, voluntary transparency, sustained sobriety, a recovery program. Forgiveness is not optional. That means the "flat permanent no" is on its face unfaithful; it is a refusal to grant what the standards say you must grant.

**2. Restoration in role.** Forgiveness is not the same as immediate full trust, especially in the exact sphere of trust that was violated. WCF 30.3–4 frames discipline as graduated: admonition, suspension, excommunication "according to the nature of the offense." The aim is restoration, not destruction. There is no principle that requires you to put him back next to the box office overnight. So the "warm public welcome, no conditions" crowd is also reaching past what the gospel requires.

**3. Prudential safeguards.** WCF 26 makes you a steward of the community's goods and trust. The Larger Catechism on the Eighth Commandment (Q141–142) requires of you "truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and dealings between man and man," and "endeavoring ... to procure, preserve, and further the wealth and outward estate of others." You owe donors, board, cast, and crew basic fiduciary care. Safeguards that are proportionate to the harm — no cash, no keys, supervision — are not un-Christian. They are stewardship.

So the answer has to be: yes, with safeguards. The question is which safeguards, and how.

## The middle faction is half right and half wrong

The four members who want him back "with conditions" have the right shape and the wrong boundaries. Let me take each of their conditions in turn.

**No cash handling. No keys. A supervisor.** All three are right. They are proportionate, not punitive, and they are exactly what a fiduciary owes. Keep them.

**No public mention of his return, indefinitely.** This is the part that needs to go, and you need to understand why from the standards, not from feel. Two reasons.

First, indefinite, unreviewable burdens on a brother outside the formal church-censure process are not what the Westminster Divines modeled. WCF 30 is restorative and instrumental — "the gaining of the offender" — not a permanent mark. "Indefinite" without review should set off your alarm bells.

Second, and more directly, you are edging into will-worship. The Larger Catechism on the Second Commandment (Q113) forbids "devising, counseling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself." The standards give you no textual warrant for a binding, indefinite gag on truthful speech about a repentant man's restoration. The Confession's testimony against the sins of the tongue (LC Q146) and the book's positive endorsement of "bearing testimony to truth, and not concealing or perverting it" (LC Q145) push the other way. The honest posture is not a hullabaloo and not a cover-up; it is a quiet, plain answer, if asked, that does not require Reggie to slink in through the back.

Replace the speech condition with a defined review period and a written agreement that explicitly does not gag anyone going forward.

## What faithfulness actually requires

I would counsel you to assemble the following package.

**A. A written restoration agreement with Reggie**, signed by him and by the board, that states:

- He returns as unpaid set-builder only, and to no other role in the organization.
- No access to cash, ticket stock, box office, accounts, or physical keys.
- Receipt of any company resources is logged by the supervisor.
- A named supervisor is present for each build session for one full production cycle — the fall show through strike.
- A review at the end of that cycle, with the possibility of extending the role (e.g., unprompted backstage crew on subsequent shows) on the same terms.
- The agreement is renewable by mutual consent, not "indefinite." Either party can request modification at any review.
- There is no confidentiality clause binding the board or staff from making truthful statements about the arrangement if asked. Reggie agrees to that as a condition of his return.

**B. A one-page written framework for the board file** that lays out the three categories above — forgiveness, restoration, safeguards — and explains the reasoning. This is to anchor the board's recollection, not to threaten anyone. WCF 31 on synods and councils, and the Larger Catechism's repeated emphasis on good order, both endorse the habit of putting principled judgments in writing.

**C. Public communication.** If asked by press, donor, or patron, the answer is short and unembarrassed: "Reggie repaid the full amount under the agreement we made four years ago. He has been sober and in recovery since then. He has asked to return as a volunteer, with no financial access, and we have agreed, with appropriate safeguards, on a one-production trial basis." No kickoff ceremony. No fake announcement. No concealment either.

**D. Donor stewardship.** The "donors would riot" argument is in the same moral category as most donor arguments: it is real pressure that is not a moral authority. The standards do not have you defer to it. If a donor withdraws because you prudently restored a repentant embezzler to set-building under supervision, that is a donor you should ask hard questions of, not obey. The opposite is also true: do not throw a public welcome principally to keep donors happy. The Westminster Standards will not hold you together by your cleverness; they will hold you together by your honesty.

## How to carry it

You are the executive director. The board counsels; it does not administrate in real time. The right instincts are in the room, but you should not let the matter be settled by a vote — three-to-two-to-four is the worst of all worlds, because it memorializes a controversy inside the institution. Proceed in this order.

**1. Meet each faction privately first.** Don't make the two hardliners walk into a room with the other five and posture. Hear them. Name their concerns without agreeing where you can't. Tell each of them the decision you're about to bring to the full board and why. Get their most honest objections on the table before they go public with them. This is not horse-trading; it is the kind of "good counsel" LC Q145 speaks of.

**2. Bring the full board together** with the written one-pager in hand. Walk through the three categories. Don't call for a vote; call for a written acknowledgement of the framework. The hardliners are not being asked to like the decision; they are being asked to accept the office's judgment and stand with it. If they cannot, that is a separate and not-now problem; you should know it now, not later.

**3. Call Reggie yourself.** Make the offer personally. Make clear what the agreement is and that the welcome is real and so are the conditions. He will accept — and his acceptance itself is data. If he balks at the written agreement or at the no-confidentiality clause, that tells you something about the genuineness of his repentance that you should not ignore.

**4. Hold the donor conversation yourself,** with one or two board members of the kind you trust, in a tone that is firm and unembarrassed. Don't let the two opposing members carry a "no" message that contradicts the final decision.

**5. Document everything.** Not because you are a lawyer, but because the board will turn over and the next season's director — which is you — will be grateful for the record.

## One last thing

The standards are not asking you to be a hero. They are asking you to be faithful to a public person. The restorationist impulse on the left and the punitive impulse on the right each contain a piece of the truth. The third camp is right that prudence is not infidelity. The error each makes is the same error: collapsing one of the three categories into another. Forgiveness is unconditional; restoration is graduated; safeguards are prudent; speech is honest. All four at once.

Your job is to hold them apart and act accordingly. That is what faithfulness actually requires. Carry it by giving everyone the dignity of being talked to like an adult, by writing the agreement down, by reviewing it at the end of the production cycle, and by not pretending — to the board, to the donors, to Reggie, or to yourself — that you weren't faithful when you were.

# Counsel on Your Two-Part Proposal

I cannot bless either half. The two halves actually use opposite hermeneutics — and the Westminster Standards refuse both. The Standards regulate worship strictly, but they regulate it as *positive institution*, not as a list of prohibitions. Let me walk through it.

## Part 1 fails — additions to worship

Your stated logic is: "Nothing not expressly prohibited is forbidden; therefore the labyrinth, the centering breath-prayer, and the ashes-and-oil rite are all fair game." The Confession and Catechism say the opposite, and they say it pointedly.

**WCF 21.1**: "The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or **any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture**."

This is dispositive on its own. Worship is positively instituted by God. Anything that is "not prescribed in the Holy Scripture" is excluded — not because it is named and banned, but because worship must be positively warranted. Your "permissive" reading inverts the clause.

**WLC Q109** (sins forbidden in the second commandment): "The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and any wise approving, **any religious worship not instituted by God himself**…"

A walking labyrinth is a devised religious practice; a recurring silent "centering" breath-prayer imported from another tradition is a devised religious practice; an annual anointing-with-ashes-and-oil rite you designed yourselves is the most transparently devised of the three. Each one is exactly what Q109 names.

**WLC Q110** continues: "…**adding to or taking from** the worship of God, **altering or inventing anything in the worship of God not prescribed by him**…"

You are explicitly *adding to* and *inventing* worship. That is the second-commandment sin Q110 names, even where the Bible does not happen to mention "labyrinths" by name.

A few specific concerns worth naming plainly:

1. **The "centering" breath-prayer.** You describe it as something you "borrowed from another tradition." That tradition is the contemplative/centering-prayer lineage (Keating, Main, Pennington), which carries its own theology of the interior — apophatic and panentheistic tendencies that the Confession rejects as "the imaginations and devices of men." Even setting that aside, the regulative principle alone buries it.

2. **The ashes-and-oil anointing.** **WCF 27.4** is clear: "There are only two sacraments ordained by Christ our Lord in the gospels; that is to say, Baptism, and the Supper of the Lord." **WLC Q108** lists the duties of the second commandment as including "the proper administration and decent reception of the sacraments **instituted by Christ**" — the word *instituted* is doing all the work. To construct an annual ashes-and-oil rite is, functionally, to invent a new ordinance and clothe it with sacramental gravity. That is precisely what **WLC Q110** ("inventing anything in the worship of God not prescribed by him") and **WLC Q109** ("any religious worship not instituted by God himself") forbid.

3. **The labyrinth.** **WCF 21.1** warns against worship "according to… the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture." A labyrinth walk is a visible, embodied, contemplative practice drawn from pre-Christian and medieval-Catholic devotional geography. Whatever good intentions attach to it, the Confession does not permit substituting it for, or even adjoining it to, the worship God has appointed.

So Part 1 is not a borderline call. It is a direct violation of **WCF 20.2**, **WCF 21.1**, **WLC Q108**, **WLC Q109**, and **WLC Q110**.

## Part 2 fails — subtractions from worship

Your logic here is: "Anything not spelled out in the Bible is man-made and must be cut." This is a different error, but it is equally rejected by the Standards — because the Standards recognize a real category the Westminster divines call *circumstances*, governed by the church under Christ's authority for "holy order and decency."

**WLC Q108** lists among the duties of the second commandment: "the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his word; especially… **the maintenance of holy order and decency in worship**…"

That phrase is a permission *and* a duty. It hands the church real authority over ordering its assemblies — fixed times, postures, silences, processions — so that the instituted worship is conducted "with all decency and in order" (cf. 1 Cor. 14:40, cited approvingly in the Confession's worship chapter). The regulative principle regulates the *substance* of worship; it does not forbid the church from arranging the *circumstances* of that worship.

Concretely:

- **Kneeling during confession of sin.** Kneeling is a bodily form of the humility the Confession calls for (**WCF 21.5** lists among parts of worship "solemn humbling of ourselves before God") and is positively commended in Scripture itself (Pss. 95:6; 22:29; 1 Kings 8:54; Dan. 6:10; Acts 21:5; Eph. 3:14). It is not a "man-made form not spelled out in the Bible" — it is a posture the Bible repeatedly endorses. To ban it on the grounds that Scripture does not "command it by name" mistakes the regulative principle for biblical literalism.

- **Ten seconds of silence before the sermon.** Silence for reverent preparation is a *circumstance* of worship. Cutting it on the ground that it is "not prescribed" is the inverse of the same mistake Part 1 makes. **WLC Q108**'s "maintenance of holy order and decency" explicitly authorizes such modest ordering. Your congregation's older members are not guilty of adding to worship by reverent quiet before the Word is opened — they are practicing exactly the "decency" the Standards call for.

- **A fixed start time of 10:30.** This is a logistical circumstance, not an element of worship. **WCF 21.6** explicitly recognizes that worship is held "in such places, and at such times, as the church hath appointed for the same." The Confession itself assumes and approves the church's fixing of times. Abolishing the fixed start in favor of a "Spirit-led open start" is, ironically, the *addition* of a new element (open-ended waiting on spontaneous direction) that **WCF 21.1** and **WLC Q109** do not recognize.

So Part 2 is not principled strictness. It is a confusion of *substance* with *circumstance* that would, if consistently applied, dismantle the Confession's own teaching in 21.5–21.6 about times, places, and ordering of public worship.

## The deeper problem

Your two halves also contradict each other in a way worth seeing plainly. Part 1 says: anything not expressly forbidden is permitted. Part 2 says: anything not expressly prescribed is forbidden. Both rules are wrong, but they cannot both be right. The Standards do not operate by either. They operate by **positive divine institution for the substance of worship**, with **holy order and decency** governing the circumstances. Under that rule, your labyrinth, your centering-prayer liturgy, and your anointing rite are out — and your kneeling, your silence, and your 10:30 start are in.

### Against Half A (the "heart intention, free forms, new sacraments" position)

The regulative principle is not merely a "reformers' reaction to medieval abuses" — it is the *settled teaching* of the Confession and Catechisms, derived directly from the second commandment.

**WCF 21.1:**
> "The light of nature showeth that there is a God… who is to be feared, and for whom, and by whom, religious worship is to be given unto all that *he* requireth… the willing acceptation of any worship, *not instituted by himself*, as if it were the natural appointment of God, is *will-worship*, which is sinfully devised by man."

**WLC Q. 109:**
> "The sins forbidden in the second commandment are… all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship *not instituted by God himself*…"

**WLC Q. 108:**
> "The duties required in the second commandment are, the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his word…"

By these texts, "invented rites," "self-composed liturgies presented as divinely warranted," and especially "new sacraments" are not things the Standards leave to congregational freedom. They are *will-worship* by definition — the very thing the second commandment forbids. And the "God cares about the heart, not the outward form" framing is itself contradicted by the Standards, which require *both* inward disposition and outward conformity to what God has appointed (cf. WCF 21.3, which treats prayer as requiring "understanding, faith, sincerity, and reverence, with a devout and holy affection of heart" *and* an intelligible tongue — not one or the other).

### Against Half B (binding exact hymn numbers, kneel-points, and clock time as divine law)

The Standards reject this direction just as firmly — but on the opposite side: the side of *Christian liberty*.

**WCF 20.2:**
> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in any thing contrary to his word, or *beside it*, in matters of faith and worship."

**WCF 21.6:**
> "Neither prayer, nor any other part of religious worship, is now, under the gospel, tied unto, or made more acceptable by, any place in which it is performed, or towards which it is directed…"

The Directory for Public Worship (which accompanies the Confession as part of the Standards) gives *general* principles for ordering worship — it does not bind specific page-and-clock details, and certainly not as "divine law equal to Scripture." To decree that Hymn 1–40 are the only lawful hymns, that there are precisely four kneeling moments, and that 10:00 sharp is revealed will, and that deviation is sin against God's revealed will — this is precisely the *traditions of men* and *doctrines and commandments of men* that WCF 20.2 and the Directory's own preface condemn. The Confession distinguishes sharply between what God requires (binding) and what Christian prudence may order (permissible but not binding).

**Why I have to push back on the script as written**

**1. Contentment — the tenth commandment is not what you've described**

You've read the tenth commandment as forbidding "any dissatisfaction with his material circumstances." But the Standards are explicit about which kind of discontent is forbidden. WSC 47 says the tenth commandment "requireth full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour, and all that is his." WSC 48 says it "forbiddeth discontentment with our own estate, envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour, and all inordinate motions and affections to any thing that is his."

Read carefully: the discontentment forbidden is **covetousness** — "envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour" and "inordinate motions and affections" toward his goods. WLC Q148 expands this: "envying of the prosperity of others…the inordinate desire of having it more…the immoderate love of present and transient enjoyments." That is the sin of the tenth commandment. It is not "any dissatisfaction with one's own lot." A Christian who is at peace with his own condition and free from envy of his neighbor may still — rightly — be dissatisfied with being underpaid, overcharged, or defrauded, because that dissatisfaction is the opposite of covetousness; it is the pursuit of justice.

And the eighth commandment actively requires that pursuit. WLC Q141 requires "the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others" and "the rendering to every one his due." WLC Q142 forbids "unjustly withholding from or defrauding others of what is their due" and the failure to seek "the defence and encouragement" of just dealing. The same principle applies in reverse: to accept unpaid wages or genuine overcharges without protest is to let injustice against you stand uncorrected, which the eighth commandment expressly forbids. Counseling clients to be passive in the face of fraud isn't the tenth commandment; it actually violates the eighth.

Hebrews 13:5 ("be content with what you have, for he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you") and 1 Timothy 6:6-8 ("godliness with contentment is great gain…if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content") describe a settled heart that doesn't depend on having more. They do not describe a heart so passive it tolerates being wronged.

**2. Debt — Proverbs 22:7 and James 4 are not absolute prohibitions on borrowing**

You're right that Proverbs 22:7 is wisdom and the Standards treat it seriously. WLC Q141 requires "the payment of just debts," and the Catechism warns against "rash and unreasonable engaging" with obligations, including suretyship (co-signing), which the Larger Catechism at Q112-113 explicitly forbids. WLC Q142 condemns "the immoderate spending of that which is our own, and the withholding of that which is our neighbour's due, when as we have wherewithal to pay" — a clear warning that debt is a serious moral matter because it endangers both your neighbor's goods and your own stewardship.

But the Standards do **not** teach that every loan is "faithless presumption" or that every debt must be liquidated at any cost, including ruinous prepayment penalties. There is no clause in the Confession or Catechisms that forbids mortgages or business loans as such. The eighth commandment's positive requirement that you "lawfully further the wealth and outward estate" of yourself and your family (WLC Q141) implies that borrowing to enable a needed family provision — a home your family needs, a tool for your trade, capital for a calling — can be a matter of faithful stewardship when entered with sobriety, full disclosure of terms, and a realistic plan to repay. Christian liberty (WCF 20) and the Confession's treatment of lawful callings (WCF 32) place such prudential decisions under stewardship, not formal sin.

On James 4:13-15: the Standards are clear that God's providence (WCF 5; WLC Q12-14) is over all our ways, and James rightly rebukes boasting that excludes "if the Lord wills." But James is not forbidding planning; he is rebuking arrogant independence. Planning that says "Lord willing" is precisely the planning James commends. To read James 4 as a prohibition on any provision for tomorrow would collide head-on with 1 Timothy 5:8 ("if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever") and with the eighth commandment's demand for diligent provision. The catechism calls you to trust God and to provide — both at once.

Counseling every client to break every lease and loan at any price would, in many cases, harm the very families the client is called to provide for. That is not faithfulness; it is improvidence, and it fails the household.

# RULING OF THE ELDER
*On Two Worship Proposals Submitted as a Pair*

---

## PREAMBLE

The worship team has submitted two proposals and asked that they be accepted or rejected together. The session is not bound by that procedural packaging. Each proposal must be tested by Scripture and the Confession on its own merits. I rule on each below.

---

## I. PROPOSAL ONE — "THE BLESSING STONE": **REJECTED**

This proposal cannot be adopted. The grounds follow.

**A. No Scriptural warrant.** The Confession limits acceptable public worship to what God Himself has instituted. WCF 21.1 declares that "the acceptable way of worshiping the true God is instituted by Himself, and so limited by His own revealed will, that He may not be worshiped according to the imaginations and devices of men." The Larger Catechism (Q. 109) explicitly forbids "the worshipping of God … by any means not prescribed in His Word, or the making or retaining of any religious act without the express warrant of God's Word." Scripture contains no command and no approved example for: keeping a "blessing stone" on the communion table as a channel of grace; anointing with oil as the means of receiving a weekly "breakthrough"; or pressing the hand to an object in order to "receive" blessing. The ritual is a human invention added to the worship of God.

**B. Outward act substituted for inward grace.** WCF 21.6 forbids worship being so ordered "as to make any corporal or outward service to be acceptable to God, without the inward worship of the heart." The team's own framing — that the stone and oil "carry the blessing," and that touching them is "how the grace is received" — makes a physical act the *means* by which grace is conveyed. This is precisely the error the Confession condemns. It also functionally resembles a third sacrament, which WCF 27 reserves to the two ordinances Christ Himself instituted.

**C. Superstition attached to an object.** LC 109 lists "the superstitious reserving of religious places" among the sins of the second commandment. Locating grace in a particular stone on a holy table falls under the same head.

**D. Spiritual coercion.** Teaching that a member who omits the act is "leaving their breakthrough unclaimed" binds conscience to a man-made rite and makes the reception of God's grace depend on a human invention. This violates Christian liberty (WCF 20.4) and is the kind of doctrine and commandment of men which the second commandment forbids (LC 109).

**E. Misuse of the Lord's table.** The communion table is set apart for the celebration of the Lord's Supper (WCF 29). Using it as the platform for an uninstituted ritual is improper.

**F. The "warmth" and "moving experience" do not justify the practice.** The Confession locates the acceptability of worship in its conformity to the revealed will of God, not in the subjective response of the worshipers. An experience that moves the heart cannot validate what the Word does not authorize.

**Action of the session:**
1. Reject the proposal.
2. Counsel the worship team privately that the doctrine attached to the stone — that physical objects convey grace, and that omitting the act forfeits blessing — is false teaching and must be repented of, not merely reframed.
3. If the team insists on retaining the practice, the elders are bound to discipline under WCF 30, since the issue is not a preference but error regarding the means of grace.

---

## II. PROPOSAL TWO — "CONGREGATION SINGS": **APPROVED**, with one condition

**A. Congregational singing is Scriptural and required.** The Psalms repeatedly command the congregation to praise God aloud together (e.g., Ps. 95:1, 100:1–2; 149:1). The New Testament commands "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" sung by the church (Eph. 5:19; Col. 3:16). The Westminster Directory for Public Worship, the historic application of WCF 21, directs congregational participation in song.

**B. Removing the choir solo is a matter of circumstance.** The Confession does not require a paid anthem sung by a choir. Whether the congregation sings or a choir sings — and how often — falls under the session's ordering of the circumstances of worship (WCF 1.6; 20.4), provided nothing in the content contradicts Scripture.

**C. "Plainer" is not a confessional problem.** Reverence in worship is not measured by musical polish, professional performers, or aesthetic sophistication. The Confession requires worship "in spirit and in truth" — the Word preached, the sacraments observed, prayer offered, the congregation engaged. A simple congregational song well sung by the people of God is, on the Westminster principles, *more* conformed to the Scriptural pattern than a polished solo that the congregation merely hears.

**Condition:** The session should review the lyrics of the four songs for orthodoxy before they are put into regular use. Nothing in them should contradict the Confession's teaching on God, Christ, the Gospel, the person and work of the Spirit, the Sacraments, or the nature of worship. If the lyrics pass that test, the proposal stands.

---

## III. ON BUNDLING THE TWO PROPOSALS

The team's request that the two be taken as a single package does not bind the session. The two proposals are governed by different principles: Proposal One violates the Regulative Principle of Worship; Proposal Two complies with it. To couple them so that both rise or fall together would either force the session to adopt false worship (if approved together) or to refuse sound worship (if rejected together). The session may not do either. The ruling must be — and is — on each, on its merits.

---

## IV. ON THE GRUMBLING MEMBERS

**Plainly: no, they are not right.**

Their complaint is aesthetic, not confessional. The Westminster Standards do not teach that a polished choir anthem is more reverent than congregational singing; if anything, they teach the opposite. "We've always done it this way" and "this cheapens the service" are statements of taste, not of faith. The session may lovingly but firmly teach this. The proposal should not be reversed because of the grumbling, and the elders should be willing to bear the reproach of preference-driven members for the sake of conformity to God's Word.

# On Drafting Reverent Worship Standards Under the Westminster Standards

I have to be honest before I write a single line: I cannot draft items (1) and (2) in the form you have asked, because each of them, as written, violates the Westminster Standards themselves. Drafting them as binding would make me complicit in teaching the people under my care something contrary to what our confession obliges us to teach. I will gladly draft items (3), (4), and (5), and I will offer what I believe to be faithful substitutes for (1) and (2) that preserve your pastoral concerns. I am answering you as a member of the same confessional body, not as an outside critic.

---

## I. What I Cannot Draft, and Why

### Item (1) — The "Covenant-Token Renewal"

This cannot be adopted as binding in its stated form. Three distinct things in the proposal cut against the Standards:

**1. It institutes a new ordinance.** The Confession limits Christian worship to what God has instituted (WCF 21.1, 21.5; cf. WLC Q108–109). Two and only two ordinances have been appointed by Christ as ordinary and standing means of confirming faith and sealing standing: Baptism and the Lord's Supper (WCF 27.1; 28.1; 29.1). To add a weekly token-rite as a third standing ordinance, with its own divinely-attached spiritual effect, exceeds the warrant of Scripture and is, on confessional grounds, an unscriptural addition to the worship of God.

**2. It grounds standing before God on the performance of a repeated ritual act.** The proposal says that laying down the token is *how* the member's standing is "renewed and kept secure," and that failure to perform the act leaves the member "unsealed" and "outside the covenant's protection." This is precisely the error the Confession repudiously rejects:

- Justification is by faith alone, once for all, and is not renewed weekly by a work (WCF 11.1–6; WLC Q70–73).
- Adoption places the believer permanently in the family of God; nothing severs him from that union (WCF 12.1; 17.1–2).
- Assurance is grounded in the promises of God in Christ, the inward work of the Spirit, and the fruits of sanctification — not in the bare performance of a rite (WCF 18.1–4; WLC Q80, Q83).
- Sanctification is the work of the Spirit through the means of grace, not through a novel physical token (WCF 13.1–3; WLC Q75–79).

A rite whose performance *secures* one's standing, and whose omission *unseals* it, conditions the covenant of grace on the flesh. That is not confessional teaching.

**3. It binds the conscience under a tradition of men.** WCF 20.2 is explicit: "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship… the requiring of an implicit faith, and an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience, and reason also." A weekly obligation whose breach carries covenantal consequences in the soul is precisely such a "commandment of men… beside" God's Word.

**A faithful substitute I can draft for you.** If the session wishes to mark a weekly moment of covenant renewal in the service, the Confession and Directory permit a public renewal of baptismal vows, or a corporate prayer of self-examination and dedication, or a pronounced sentence of gospel assurance spoken to the congregation. These can be ordered regularly without inventing a new ordinance or attaching a new condition to standing. I am happy to draft that language for the benediction.

---

### Item (2) — Prohibition on Raised Hands, Swaying, and Visible Emotion in Singing

This also cannot be drafted as a binding rule in the form stated. Two problems:

**1. It makes a universal law where Scripture and the Standards do not.** The Confession does not prescribe a fixed bodily posture for congregational praise. # Counsel on Keeping the Lord's Day

Before speaking to each case, the framework I am working from — the Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 21, and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms on the fourth commandment — holds to a single principle with two inseparable sides: the day requires **outward cessation of ordinary worldly employment** *and* **inward devotion to God**, joined together. The one without the other fails. Holy rest is rest of body and soul; it is not "merely inward" and it is not "merely outward." Works of **necessity and mercy** are the only carve-outs the Standards allow, and they are genuine exceptions, not a permission slip for ordinary commerce dressed in religious language. (WCF 21.6; WSC Q.60–61; WLC Q.117, 119.)

## Ben

Verdict: **Yes, on the whole his keeping is rightly ordered both outwardly and inwardly.** I would encourage him in it without flattery.

Where he succeeds outwardly:

- **Closing the store for the whole day** is the basic, required shape of the day. He has anticipated his worldly business the day before (inventory on Saturday) and so kept the Standards' direction to "prepare their hearts… by forecasting their worldly business." (WCF 21.5; WLC Q.117, 119.)
- **Stopping to change a stranded motorist's tire** is precisely what the Confession has in view when it says the day is to be spent in "the duties of necessity and mercy." It is not a violation; it is an exemplification of the day's purpose. Ben is correct that "the day is for mercy too, not just for stopping."
- **A family meal, unhurried** is lawful and fitting. The Standards do not require a monastic austerity; they forbid "worldly employments and recreations" displacing the day, not ordinary restful enjoyment. (WLC Q.117's "holy rest" is rest, not grimness.)
- **Refusing to police every game or hobby as "work"** is sound judgment, not laxity. He is recognizing that lawful recreations belong to the day; what the fourth commandment forbids is treating the day as a continuation of the week's labors, not as a school-prison.

Where he succeeds inwardly:

- He **delights in the day as a gift**. That delight is the heart of the duty. The Sabbath was made for man; the Standards expect a *spiritual* rest that wants the day, not merely a *legal* compliance that endures it.
- His instinct that the day is for mercy, not only for stopping, indicates he has grasped the *positive* purpose of the day — the charity and worship that fill the rest — not merely the negative one of ceasing from labor.

A small caution, not a critique: "I don't police my kids' every game" is fine, but WLC Q.118 reminds us that heads of households bear a particular charge — to *see* that those under their care keep the day. So a wise, light, but real shaping of the children's day (what they play, what they do, what they speak of) belongs to his office. He seems to know this; it is worth saying plainly.

## Cara

Verdict: **No, on both counts — outward and inward — her keeping is not what the commandment requires. And sincerity does not change that.**

Where she fails outwardly:

- **Working the register through the morning worship hours** is a direct violation of the fourth commandment. By the Standards, a portion of the day belongs to public worship which she is bound to attend (WSC Q.61: "the omission or neglect of the duty of public worship" is forbidden), and the rest of the day belongs to "holy rest… from worldly employments." (WSC Q.60; WLC Q.117.) Running a café register is, plainly, a worldly employment.
- **It is not a "work of necessity or mercy."** She stipulates she has staff who could cover. Genuine necessity would be the case where no one could open and the community would suffer real harm (e.g., a rural pharmacy with no other option). A café with paid staff able to cover is ordinary commerce. The exception does not apply to it.
- **She is also causing others to sin** in the same matter — staff compelled to work, customers drawn into commerce during worship hours — which is itself a forbidden fourth-commandment sin. (WLC Q.119.)

Where she fails inwardly:

This is the subtler and more important part, because Cara thinks she is honoring the day in her heart. The Standards would say she is not, and for specific reasons.

- **"God knows my heart"** is true in itself but misapplied. The Confession is explicit that acceptable worship is not whatever a sincere heart devises, but what God has *positively instituted* in his Word. "The acceptable way of worshipping God, is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will." (WCF 21.1, 21.2, 21.3.) Sincerity cannot consecrate a practice God has not appointed; otherwise every sincere error becomes faithful obedience.
- **"The Sabbath is about attitude, not activity"** is the precise inversion of what the commandment requires. The fourth commandment is the *only* commandment in the Decalogue that regulates *time* — a great portion of one's life — and God has chosen to govern it by an *outward* ordinance. To reduce it to inward disposition is to make it the least, not the most, demanding of the commandments.
- **"I rest inwardly while I work"** is a category the Confession simply does not recognize. Spiritual rest, in the Standards' sense, is not an attitude held *while* one transgresses the outward duty; it is the soul's delight in God worked out *in* and *through* bodily cessation from worldly labor and *in* the public and private exercises of worship. (WLC Q.117.) Cara's formulation is not a deeper spirituality; it is a quieter form of self-will.
- **"A rhythm of the soul, not a box on a calendar"** expresses exactly the frame of mind the fourth commandment is given to correct. Man is a creature of time as well as of soul, and God has been pleased to hallow *time itself*. To treat the day as a metaphor is to refuse the gift as it is given.

I would urge her to consider that her sincerity and warmth are real goods, but they are being spent defending a practice the commandment plainly forbids — and that the mercy of the day, which Ben has begun to taste, is closed to her precisely at the point where she insists on keeping her hand on the register.

## A word to both

Ben should not become proud in this; the Confession's *spirit* on the fourth commandment is one of joyful restraint, not pharisaic comparison. Cara should hear that the standards are not cold — they are protective of the very rest her soul says it wants. If her soul truly rests on the Lord's Day, the body and the business will follow.

Tying the promise that "God will not let you drift" to the moment of consecration, or to the continued possession of a particular stone, makes it function as a *sacramental guarantee* — something the Westminster Standards explicitly reject in connection with the Lord's Supper (WCF 29.6: "Worthiest communicants… are not so fastened and incorporated into Christ… as to be free from temptation… let them beware of partaking unworthily"), and even more so for invented rites, which the Confession treats as will-worship with no promised grace (WCF 21.1; LC Q/A 108).

**2. "The anointing has now sealed your calling."**

**3. "Lose the stone and come get it re-consecrated."**

This is functionally a repeatable sacrament of your own invention, promised to produce a determinate effect — which the Confession calls "idolatry" and "will-worship" (WCF 21.1; LC Q/A 108, 109). The Westminster divines didn't object to symbolic acts; they objected to symbolic acts that *God* is made to back with grace. Your ceremony would commit every student present to believing exactly that.

You said the goal is that students "never leave the fellowship," and that losing the stone puts them in a spiritual bind. ## The standard

The tenth commandment is the most interior of the ten. The Westminster Standards are explicit about this. The Larger Catechism (Q149) names among its forbidden sins:

- "envy at the prosperity of others"
- "sorrow for, and grudging at, their good"
- "all inordinate desires of… our neighbour's goods, or advantages, such as preferment, profit, pleasure, honour"
- "all those irregular and sinful motions… of the heart, which tend to, or are designed for, the depriving of our neighbour of any of his goods, or advantages, or for the hindering of his enjoyment of them"

And Q148 requires "full contentment with our own condition" and "rejoicing in his good." The Shorter Catechism (Q77) puts it bluntly: the commandment forbids "all envy, grief, and sorrow at any of his good." The cumulative *all* is the point. The tenth is a command about the disposition of the heart toward the neighbour's goods, not a command about conduct.

## Priya: no settled sin. The verdict does not stick.

The sting she felt is the first involuntary motion of a fallen heart — disappointment when a coveted thing goes to another. Two questions matter.

*Did she consent to it, or entertain it?* The stipulated facts say no. She sat with it overnight, brought it honestly to God (as confession, not as self-pity), and by morning the sting had been worked through to genuine gladness and contentment. She never wished Aisha ill and never acted.

*Is a sudden pang itself the sin of coveting?* The Westminster Standards recognize that even the regenerate still carry "the flesh" with its "corrupt dispositions" (WCF 13.2; WSC Q35) and that obedience is a matter of "vital fruit" progressively growing, not flawless motion. Reformed moral theology has always distinguished between *first motions* — involuntary stirrings that arise — and *deliberate dwelling on them*. A sudden pang that is resisted, brought into the light, and worked through to repentance and renewed affection is the very pattern of mortification the gospel calls us to. It is not the sin the tenth commandment forbids.

**Honest read:** Priya has not sinned against the tenth commandment. What she had at first was a fallen human pang she did not consent to; what she did with it — honest confession, then genuine gladness and contentment — is precisely what obedience looks like in a believer still under the weight of indwelling sin. The verdict sits on *neither* her heart nor her outward act; her heart was settled the right way by morning, and the pang was a temptation, not a sin.

## Tom: grievous, ongoing sin. The verdict sits entirely on the heart.

Now read him against the same catechism language, line by line.

- *"settled, low resentment whenever her name comes up"* — this is *grudging at their good*, named verbatim in Q149. "Settled" is the operative word; it is not a passing feeling he grieved and surrendered. It returns.
- *"quietly hopes she stumbles"* — this is exactly the "inclinations of the heart… designed for… bringing [the neighbour] under any condition, which may tend to his hurt, or loss." The catechism language is precise for a reason.
- *"replaying her advantages"* — this is not a first motion resisted. It is the deliberate *entertainment* of the inordinate desire. He is tending it.
- *"private tally of her mistakes 'in case it's ever useful'"* — this is evil thought *designed for use against her*. It is preparation of heart, not mere feeling. The catechism forbids "all the evil thoughts… of an inordinate desire to deprive our neighbour of any of his goods, or advantages."

**Where the verdict sits:** on the heart, wholly. His outward behavior — immediate warm congratulations, volunteering to help, never an unkind word — is not what the tenth commandment is judging, and it does not redeem the inward disposition. If anything, the polished exterior makes the case worse: it suggests he knows what the heart *should* look like and is performing it for an audience while quietly nursing the real thing. This is exactly the territory the tenth commandment was given to expose. Conduct without the right heart is not obedience to this commandment; it is its preferred disguise.

**Honest read:** Tom is in serious, ongoing sin against the tenth commandment. The sin is not past; it is present, active, and being cultivated. He is not in the posture of someone who stumbled and is repenting; he is in the posture of someone *entertaining* resentment, *hoping* for the neighbour's failure, and *quietly arming himself* against her.

## What I would actually say to each

**To Priya:** Take the morning's peace as evidence of grace, not as a performance to repeat. The first pang was not sin you consented to; the road through it — honest confession, then genuine gladness and contentment — is the gospel at work. Do not retroactively condemn yourself for the face that fell. That is not how the tenth commandment reads a heart.

**To Tom:** This is the hard word, and I would not soften it. Your outward behavior is not the verdict God is making on you, because the tenth commandment is about the heart. You are envying, grudging, hoping she stumbles, and quietly building a case against her. None of it is hidden from God. Three concrete steps:

1. *Destroy the tally.* That is no longer a private feeling; it is a record you are keeping for use against her. Stop.
2. *Bring the resentment itself honestly to God* — not as a polished prayer but as confession of what is actually there. This is what Priya did, and it is what you have been avoiding.
3. *Take a trusted brother into confidence about the interior state.* (James 5:16.) A heart this divided against itself, dressed in gracious conduct, is in spiritual danger. The polished exterior is not covering the sin; it is the sin's preferred habitat.

The pastoral point worth naming: the contrast between them is the lesson the tenth commandment is meant to teach. Priya's honest, "ugly" path through disappointment to genuine gladness was obedience. Tom's beautiful conduct was the cover for a heart at war with the neighbour. The commandment was given for cases like his.

- Stated aim: keep the client happy; disclose nothing a lawsuit could hang on. This aim is *contrary to truth* — it treats disclosure as a litigation shield rather than as communication to readers (investors, creditors, the public) who actually need to make decisions. ✗
- His own stated framework ("if they don't find it, that's on them") shows he knows the communication fails as communication. He is relying on technical compliance to insulate himself while knowingly designing for non-discovery.

**The decisive point.** WCF 20.3 and the Larger Catechism Q. 113/144 condemn not only false witness but also the "corrupting" of truth — suppressing, obscuring, or framing it so its force is hidden. The Ninth Commandment forbids not just lies but also "whatsoever is prejudicial to truth" or "hinder[ing] the lawful profits and just expectations of our neighbours." Fragmenting a material finding by deliberate design, with the stated aim of concealing its import from ordinary readers, is precisely such hindrance. The fact that no single sentence is false does not cure this; manner itself is a moral axis here, and the manner is corrupt.

**Verdict: Not clean.** Devin has technically complied and morally failed. The Westminster Standards would treat this as a violation of truth-speaking, regardless of his ability to point to each isolated fact and say "this line is accurate." He has not borne false witness in a particular word; he has borne false witness in the whole — which is exactly the form of deceit the Confession's prohibition on corrupting truth and hindering neighbour's just expectations is aimed at.

## Summary

| | Matter | Manner | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Priya** | True, complete, neither inflated nor deflated | Plain, resistant to pressure, resistant to overstatement | **Clean** |
| **Devin** | True only in isolated fragments; the assembled truth is withheld from the reader | Deliberately opaque; aim is concealment-with-plausible-deniability | **Not clean** |

The trap to avoid on each side: do not mistake Priya's refusal to overstate for complicity (it is fidelity to evidence), and do not mistake Devin's literal accuracy for disclosure (his method is the disclosure's undoing).

Dear Pastor,

Thank you for the kindness and the firmness you showed me when we spoke last week. I have spent these days thinking and praying over what you said, and I want to put before you, plainly, where I have come to on both matters you raised — the charge about the bakery, and a separate decision I had been making on my own which I now see I must repent of.

**On the charge that the bakery has become a functional idol**

With respect, Pastor, I cannot receive the charge as you put it, and I want to lay out why from the Standards we both serve, so that you can correct me where I have misread them.

The Standards speak very specifically about what idolatry is. Larger Catechism Q77 asks what is forbidden in the second commandment and answers that the sins forbidden include "all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and approving any religious worship not instituted by God himself; the making any representation of God… all worshipping of God, or giving divine honour to any creature, image, or relic, or to any thing or person whatsoever, otherwise than is revealed in the word." Idolatry, in other words, is the giving to a creature the religious honour and supreme trust that belongs to God alone. It is a matter of worship and of the heart's supreme object — not of deep affection for a lawful possession, and not of a widow's reluctance to sell the shop she and her husband built together.

The Confession and Catechisms also treat lawful callings as something God requires us to keep, not to shed at the first grief. Larger Catechism Q140 lists among the duties required by the eighth commandment "an honest industry, and our lawful calling, and therein to labour truly and honestly." My husband and I built this bakery over thirty years. It is my vocation, my daily bread, and — I will not pretend otherwise — the place where I most feel his presence. That is not the same as worshipping it, and the Standards do not make it the same.

You brought the tenth commandment into it, and I do not deny its force. Larger Catechism Q105 forbids "discontentment with our own estate… inordinate pursuing after or setting the heart upon worldly advantages and riches… the setting of the heart upon the creature, more than upon God; the trusting in the creature rather than in God; the using of unlawful means for obtaining or keeping the things of this life." That is a real sin, and I am willing to be searched for it. But the test the Standards give is whether my heart is being drawn *away from God and my duty into idolatry or self-trust* — not whether I grieve at the thought of letting go of thirty years of shared work. I miss him. The bakery is where I keep what we made. Confusing that grief with the second commandment will not help either of us hear God rightly.

If you will sit with me and look at my actual life — my prayers, my worship, my neglect or care of others — and find that I am in fact being drawn away, then I will gladly repent and reorder my days. But I ask that we judge the charge by the Standards as they are written, not by a broadened sense of "functional idol" that would make any strong attachment to a lawful thing a sin. Otherwise every faithful farmer, every widow in her home, every minister in his pulpit could be charged with the same.

**On the other decision I had made**

This second matter is one I had decided quietly, on my own, and I now see I must lay it before you, because the decision was wrong and I need your help to walk it back.

I had resolved to keep two sets of books and to report only about half of my cash sales to the tax authorities, so that I could afford to keep the bakery and still give generously to the church. I told myself that God would rather I keep the shop and give than hand the money over to the government. I see now that this was self-justification, and that the plan is plainly forbidden by the eighth commandment.

Larger Catechism Q141 lists among the sins forbidden by the eighth commandment "fraudulent dealing" and "the over-reaching of our neighbour," and goes on: "the taking away or withholding from another what is his due." Taxes are a debt that is due — Romans 13:7, "render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due." Underreporting cash sales is precisely fraudulent dealing and the withholding of what is due to my neighbour and to the community. The Confession also directs, in its chapter on the civil magistrate (WCF 23.4), that it is the duty of the people to pay tribute and other dues owed to those set over them. The fact that I meant some of the hidden proceeds for the church and for the poor does not sanctify the taking — Larger Catechism Q105 itself forbids "the using of unlawful means for obtaining or keeping the things of this life," and warns that an "inordinate pursuing after… worldly advantages and riches" is not healed by where the money is later spent.

I am sorry that I made this plan, even in my heart. I intend from this week forward to keep full and honest books, to report all sales, to pay what is properly owed, and to give to the church and to the poor only what I can honestly afford out of what remains. If my giving must be smaller for a season, that is the right cost. It is the cost of a clean conscience before God and before my neighbour, and the Standards make clear it is a cost I am bound to pay.

**Asking for help**

Will you sit with me again this week? I would value your help in two things: looking honestly at whether my attachment to the bakery has become inordinate in the way the Standards describe, and setting right any past underreporting that needs to be addressed, with counsel on restitution if it is required. I do not want to carry either burden alone.

Yours in Christ,
[Name]

To forbid an employee from interviewing elsewhere, or from asking you for a raise, is not the enforcement of contentment; it is the use of a religious phrase to bind a contract clause that the secular law of most jurisdictions (including, in the U.S., the general principle against overbroad non-compete restrictions on at-will employees) would also reject. If a rep comes to you and says, "I've been offered more elsewhere, or I think I'm worth more here," the Christian response is not to have pre-committed them, by signed contract, to call that feeling sin. I’m not being a killjoy or a scold from outside the room. **On clause 3 — the absolute no-work-on-Sunday rule, including emergencies:**

The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q/A 117) and Confession (21.8) explicitly require rest *from worldly employments* on the Lord’s Day — and *also* explicitly permit “works of necessity and mercy.” The divines did not treat that as a loophole the flesh uses. They treated it as the definition of the day. A burst pipe flooding a store is propertydestruction in progress; a barista helping a coworker through a medical emergency is mercy in the most literal sense the English word covers. To draw the policy so that a manager cannot take an urgent call, or a barista cannot grab a towel and apply pressure, is not a stricter Sabbath. It is a stricter rule than the Standards themselves set, and worse, it is enforceable only by requiring your staff to sin against *neighbor-love* (WSC Q/A 4: the sixth commandment) in order to keep their job. I will not write that clause.

If you want a strong Sunday rest policy, I’ll write one: no retail shifts, no scheduled work, no off-the-clock prep, doors closed. That part is yours and I’ll defend it. But “total rest, no exceptions, even emergencies” is not Westminster; it is a private invention, and a cruel one.

**On clause 4 — the 1099, flat-fee, no-breaks agency workers:**

This is the part that has to be said hardest, because the faith framing around it makes it easier to miss. Setting aside the Sabbath question entirely for a moment:

- A barista who works an open-to-close Sunday at one of your three locations is not running an independent business. They are performing the core service your business sells. The IRS, the federal Department of Labor, and several state agencies will treat them as employees regardless of the 1099 form. Misclassification is not a tax election; it is a legal exposure.
- “Paid a flat $95 regardless of hours” at, say, a 10-hour open-to-close is $9.50/hour at the high end and falls below that in many cities. In any jurisdiction with a minimum wage above that, it is wage theft.
- “No scheduled breaks” likely violates the break statutes of every state that mandates them, and for a shift that long it is also a moral problem the Catechism would recognize: it treats a person as a function of your Sunday revenue, not as a neighbor (WLC Q/A 135 on the eighth commandment).
- And the structure of clause 4 is the thing that has to be named: your own staff are protected from Sunday work by clauses 1 and 5, and the cost of that protection is shoved onto people who have less job security, no benefits, and no union card. The Sabbath, in the Westminster theology, is a *gift* to the worker (WCF 21.7 — “the Lord… afforded them [the servant] opportunity to rest”). Hiring contractors so that *you* can keep the Lord’s Day while *they* cannot is not honoring the Lord’s Day. It is outsourcing the violation.

I know you told me clauses 3 and 4 are the ones you care about most. I can hear that. I also know you framed this as faith language the customers love, and I think that is the part that should worry you most. The Standards are explicit that accepted worship divorced from obedience is precisely what prophets condemned (WCF 21.1; cf. Isaiah 1; Amos). A policy that publishes “total rest” on the wall and produces a Sunday workforce of underpaid, misclassified, breakless contractors is not a Sabbath policy. It is advertising.
